speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to move a motion under Standing Order 43 to discuss a matter of urgent national importance-the report of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics yesterday that during the third quarter of this year, which has just ended, the country experienced the highest rate of unemployment it has had in any similar period since the latter days of the great depression of the 1930's; and particularly, the refusal of the government to introduce positive measures to stimulate the economy, and the refusal of ministers, particularly those with economic portfolios, to be present in the House when this important matter is being discussed to listen to the suggestions put forward by the elected representatives of the people for combating serious and rising unemployment.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
I therefore move, under Standing Order 43, that this matter be brought before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, where expert witnesses from the fields of industry and labour can be called to make positive suggestions to the government for dealing with this very serious situation, in the hope that these suggestions will be paid attention to and acted upon without delay.

subsubtopic: PAKISTAN-ASSISTANCE TO CYCLONE AND FLOOD VICTIMS

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED LACK OF POLICIES AND PROGRAMS TO PREVENT UNEMPLOYMENT, POVERTY AND SOCIAL INJUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, without question we are faced with the most difficult winter that we have had in years, both from the point of view of employment and the economy. The realization just now seems to have hit the government, probably too late. Despite the growing promises in the Speech from the Throne and in the hundreds of speeches that cabinet ministers have made all over the country, Parliament and the government are in neutral gear. We have done nothing but talk about the situation in Quebec, urged on by rumours originating from government sources.
Even if we had set all that aside, there is practically nothing on the Order Paper for us to consider that would do anything to meet the emergency situation. Just now we had an outline of the business to be dealt with within the next week, and it is a dismal effort as far as any measures to improve the economy or to relieve the employment situation are concerned. Just look at the 20 pieces of legislation on the order paper right now. There is hardly one job creator in the whole lot. There are bills concerning the labelling of products, statistics publication, cutting the powers of the Auditor General, amendments to the Customs Tariff, and so forth. Then, we should look at this week's accomplishments so far as this Parliament is concerned. Monday and Tuesday we spent on the public order temporary measures bill. Yesterday and today, we have the special debate to urge some action to relieve the unemployment situation. Tomorrow, we will not be sitting. That does not give any feeling of confidence to those who are watching this government and Parliament in our ability to meet an emergency situation.
In my opinion the time has come for us in the House to face up to the ridiculous and tragic situation to which we and our country have been brought. A couple of dozen revolutionaries in Montreal have made fools of the Canadian government and the Canadian people. They have panicked the government into declaring a state of war or insurrection. They have frightened the life out of everyone in Quebec. They have given the rest of Canada a national emotional binge. They have eluded the police for six weeks, although apparently they are still around the city of Montreal. They have caused Canada to lose its high standing internationally, and Quebec to lose millions of dollars economically. The government of Canada has played into their hands right down the line, and we look more foolish as the days go by.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
We have spent six weeks of Parliament's time in discussing the War Measures Act and the temporary public order bill while the nation's economy is crashing down around us, the unemployed are walking the streets in increasing thousands, and pollution is continuing to choke us and ruin our heritage. Sitting in this House during the six weeks since the session began has been among my most saddening and frustrating experiences here.
Employment Programs
As we watch unemployment and misery in Canada mount, as the number of letters sent to members looking for help and jobs increases, and as the economy deteriorates the government has sat apparently helpless, and without policy or action. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has concerned himself almost entirely with the political situation in Quebec. The rest of Canada must wait.
The Prime Minister has indicated no concern, in any remarks he has made in this House or outside it, about the human misery, or unemployment. They are only figures on a chart. I do not know when the people of the country are going to wake up to the fact that they are being distracted from their misery by a series of confrontations in the province of Quebec. Probably that will come when the Prime Minister's opponents in Quebec become tired of being the whipping boys every time he wants to bolster his image in the rest of Canada.
Within the past few days, the government has indicated that it will allot extra money for the creation of employment this winter. But it is well known that suddenly making money available will not create jobs. You cannot just go out and build a new factory, or create a demand for goods and services in a few weeks. It takes not weeks but months, and in some cases years. The demand for goods and services, for increased production and the reversing of lay-offs in industry, cannot be met unless money is available to the public to buy goods. The tight money policy of the past few months has left less money in people's pockets with which to buy goods and services. Certainly, Mr. Speaker, you do not increase your purchasing power from unemployment insurance or welfare cheques.
So far as inflation is concerned the government itself may be a strong contributing factor. Just today the Miscellaneous Estimates Committee was presented with supplementary estimates for the current year showing an increase of $457 million, almost an extra half billion dollars. Our total federal spending is now $13,355,000,000, but so far as we could learn this morning only $60 million is for job creation this winter, that is $60 million of that $457 million. The $17 million was for student employment last summer. This large increase in government spending can do nothing but increase the inflationary trend unless it is used substantially for job creation, and that certainly does not appear to be the case from the figures presented to that committee. The government is now forecasting a budgetary deficit of some $400 million this fiscal year instead of a surplus of $200 million. It is finally recognizing, to some degree at least, the desperate situation we face this winter.
The extra money being spent would be justified if it were shown that it was being used to create jobs, but this does not appear to be the case. So, the increase in expenditure of half a billion dollars is not to fight unemployment, as is often recommended, but is merely an increase in general spending by the government, an increase which the public will have to meet by way of taxes, which will reduce by that amount the money they have available for purchases.

November 19, 1970
Employment Programs
I would like to look for a few minutes at unemployment prospects for this winter. Unemployment affects the different regions of Canada differently yet, as obvious as that might be, government policy is not tempered by this reality. Apparently the government is obsessed with controlling inflation. However, that applies to everybody else except the government. So far as its expenditures are concerned inflation continues to rise.
British Columbia at present has a rate of unemployment which is higher than the national average. The rate there is predicted to peak this winter with over 13 per cent of its work force unemployed. The highly seasonal nature of employment in the forestry sector accounts for some of this unemployment, and recently the Economic Council has cited the heavy incidence of industrial strikes as another reason for the unemployment picture. Yet this province rightly boasts of one of the best educated work forces in the country, and the highest per capita income in Canada.
The Prairie region traditionally has the lowest level of unemployment of any area in the country. It is worth noting then, Mr. Speaker, that the forecast actual rate of unemployment, set at 8 per cent for this region this winter, is almost double what the area normally experiences. In addition, there is reason to believe that there is considerable hidden unemployment in the Prairies, since the labour force figures omit farmers idled by a slowdown in farm production. Furthermore, it is obvious that the "government's left hand doesn't know what the right's doing"; regional policy has been particularly lamentable for this region.
The government of Manitoba has estimated that that Province has lost more jobs because of the government's closing of certain military bases and the moving of Air Canada's repair facilities to Montreal, than the province has gained through the government's regional incentive programs. The government is trying to pump funds into certain areas to repair the damage it has done itself. As I said previously, Mr. Speaker, pumping money into an area cannot create jobs immediately, or even in the near future. It seems that the quickest way of producing work for people has always been, and will continue to be, through the municipalities and local governments. All of these governments have on their shelves many projects which could usefully be done during the winter months.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
In previous years of high unemployment, special projects or winter works have been undertaken with federal and local co-operation. This means that even if a man does not have a permanent job he will be able to go out and do something, giving himself the satisfaction of earning money to keep himself and his family. This could very easily be done through a winter works program but the government has rejected it time and again-perhaps because it was originally a policy of the former Progressive Conservative government. If that is the reason it is a most lamentable situation, because this is where some help could reach those badly in need this winter.
To come now to Ontario, which is the traditional beneficiary of government money and fiscal policies, this centre, under the government's national policy, will not be helped this winter. Peak unemployment is headed for a ten-year high of 7 per cent in Ontario. In some areas within the province local unemployment will be twice the provincial average.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED LACK OF POLICIES AND PROGRAMS TO PREVENT UNEMPLOYMENT, POVERTY AND SOCIAL INJUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I would respectfully recommend to the federal government that when the federal and provincial finance ministers meet in Ottawa on December 7 and 8 to compare notes on the economy and to exchange information on the economic prospects for the next year, the federal government initiate discussions with the provinces immediately on the unemployment situation. They should also discuss joint initiatives that the two levels of governments could take to meet the crisis situation of the jobless in Canada this winter. I understand that most provinces are willing, and indeed quite anxious, to take part in such discussions. I feel it is incumbent upon this government to initiate the studies with the provincial finance ministers when they meet here on December 7 and 8.
This winter Canadians appear to be facing the most severe unemployment crisis since the great depression of the 1930's. According to economists and people eminently qualified to speak on the subject, it is expected that one out of every ten Canadians in the country's labour force will be out of a job by March of next year. This is a very very serious prospect. Should this happen, 750,000 to 800,000 men and women and their families will be facing a bitter struggle for economic survival in the months ahead.

It is quite apparent, Mr. Speaker, that, as
pointed out by the previous speaker, this government has been so preoccupied with Quebec terrorism and the FLQ that it has all but lost sight of the bitter economic crisis that Canada faces this winter. While it is not my intention to criticize the government's action in Quebec in recent weeks and months, I suggest to them and to the House that there are problems facing Canadians far more serious than the FLQ in Quebec. These are the problems connected with being able to keep body and soul together during the coming winter and are a result of this government's illogical and completely insane policies to fight inflation which have had a ruinous effect on the economy of this country to the grief and sorrow of the average man, the unemployed, the untrained, the underemployed and the little people of Canada generally.
Instead of dealing with unemployment with the same vigour and enthusiasm, and the same degree of urgency

November 19, 1970

that has been applied to imposing law and order in Quebec, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his colleagues have been groping around like blind men, groping around in a daze as though they do not really believe that things are going to be very bad in Canada during the coming winter. They have used the old ostrich psychology of sticking their heads in the sand and pretending all is well.
I feel that this House and Canadians generally, Mr. Speaker, should demand, must demand, that this government treat the coming winter unemployment as an emergency, and must produce emergency measures to deal with it.

speechtext:
Whether the government wishes to
acknowledge this fact or not, it does have a moral obligation to deal with this problem which has been created to a large extent by its own illogical and irrational inflationary policies of the past year and a half.
The unemployment situation in Canada is a continuing embarrassment to the government's fight against inflation. The House knows that the embarrassment is much more acute when the unemployment figures are released by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. The result is that the government has developed a method of presenting unemployment figures which makes them appear better than they are. I might say that it is quite obvious to most members, and I am quite sure to the Canadian public, that the government has actually succeeded in fooling itself by its own figures. However, I am sure they are not fooling the average man and certainly they are not fooling the large number of Canadians who now find themselves unemployed or are facing the prospect of unemployment during the coming winter months.
Economists tell us that by February, 1971, an estimated three-quarters of a million Canadians will be out of work. Donald MacDonald, President of the Canadian Labour Congress, has predicted that by February our unemployment figures will reach 9 per cent. Other observers have predicted that the rate could go as high as 14 per cent for the same period.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED LACK OF POLICIES AND PROGRAMS TO PREVENT UNEMPLOYMENT, POVERTY AND SOCIAL INJUSTICE
speechtext:
It appears that this government has an obsession with inflation, Mr. Speaker. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) and the Prime Minister have embarked upon a program of economic policies that guarantee no assurance of success and no assurance that they can beat inflation without having a ruinous effect on the economy.
The unfortunate aspect of this government's folly is that the people who contribute less to inflation, the untrained, the unemployed, the people who are barely scraping a living, the widows and the orphans and the people on the welfare rolls, are the real victims of this government's anti-inflationary policy.
Employment Programs
What we need in Canada, Mr. Speaker, is an economic policy which is devoted to growth and full employment for all Canadians. It is unfortunate that our country, which boasts of having the second or third highest per capita income in the world, should have such a high degree of poverty. The elimination of the disparity between our "haves" and "have-nots" presents a monumental challenge to our leaders, but unfortunately the present government has failed in its mandate and has been unable or unwilling to meet this challenge.
The fourth report recently published by the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council has revealed some startling statistics with regard to the economic conditions of the Atlantic region. For example, it is said, I believe, that in 1969 one person in four in Atlantic Canada was either unemployed or employed on some job that paid very low wages which were barely sufficient to keep body and soul together. We also find that conditions were such in Atlantic Canada between 1956 and 1969 that there was a mass exodus of people from that area. Indeed 209,000 people-I repeat, 209,000 people-were forced because of economic conditions to move from the Atlantic area between 1956 and 1969. This, I believe, underlines the serious weakness of the economy of that region. Newfoundland lost 54,000 people in the same period. Other Atlantic provinces lost large numbers of people they could not afford to lose.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
It appears, Mr. Speaker, that the difficulties were brought about because this government refused to acknowledge that Canada is made up of four or five different areas or regions. Instead, it has adopted the same policies right across the country in fighting inflation and unemployment. Quite obviously, the government ought to adopt regional policies for dealing with the difficulties in each of the regions. It is sheer madness to expect the Prairies and the Atlantic provinces to pay the price for the government's fight against inflation when those regions are already suffering their worst unemployment in years. The result of the government's policies in fighting inflation is economic chaos, and complete and utter frustration in the provinces that are affected most. I think I am not exaggerating when I say that the Atlantic region has probably been affected more by the government's anti-inflation policies than any part of Canada, with the exception of Quebec perhaps.
I should like to make a few proposals which the government may wish to consider and implement in the months ahead. They may help to alleviate the very serious difficulties brought about by unemployment. I strongly recommend that the benefits payable to all eligible unemployed persons be increased, to alleviate the distress that has been caused to many by the loss of their jobs. Families without any weekly income need money now, and not in two months time or whenever the white paper of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) will be implemented. They need money now, because their chances of gaining employment are growing slimmer every week.

November 19, 1970
Employment Programs
I also recommend that the government should increase the funds available under the Canada Assistance Plan. Reports from many cities indicate that municipal funds in this field are all but exhausted. This indicates clearly that there is a great need for more money, which ought to be distributed to the provinces under the Canada Assistance Plan.
I urge the government to remove financial constraints from the construction industry. Canadians need homes; yet the number of workers in the building industry has declined this year to a greater extent than is customary. The decline this year has been greater than in any year In the past decade.
I call on the government to remove the doubt existing in the minds of many Canadians, many businessmen both large and small, relating to the matter of tax reform in order that industry may have the necessary information with which to finance new development and order new construction. We have seen the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) dancing and working around the problem; I am afraid that has been of little consolation to the average Canadian or to the average Canadian businessman, big or small. There is a certain amount of doubt as to how tax reform will affect business.
I also ask the government to cease its attacks on organized labour.

Let it stop using labour as the sacrificial lamb of inflation, because this is what it is doing. We need the co-operation of labour, and I am sure this co-operation could be achieved if a new climate were created by this government. Instead of trying to pin the responsibility for what is happening on labour, let us try to get together with labour and work out the means whereby we can help each other to create a new climate.
I strongly urge the government to support the construction of urban transit projects. Most cities have in existence detailed urban transit plans; all they are requesting is the money to put those plans into effect. I ask the government to inaugurate immediately, in consultation with the provinces and municipalities, plans under which we can start work on sewage treatment plants and other anti-pollution measures.
Programs such as I have enumerated are intended to create new jobs and new job opportunities. Such programs, working through the public and private sector, would stimulate the economy and hence, of course, increase the demand for labour. Regionalized winter works and house construction would also provide additional stimulus to the regions. Accelerated transfers to provincial governments would enable those governments to meet their commitments. I also ask the government to step up grants under the regional industrial incentives program.
I heard an hon. member yesterday refer to the industrial incentives program, and he spoke as though this
program were the answer to all our problems. I ask him to reconcile his position, that these programs are the answer to all our difficulties, which the high rate of unemployment from which we suffer at present.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Marchand (Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED LACK OF POLICIES AND PROGRAMS TO PREVENT UNEMPLOYMENT, POVERTY AND SOCIAL INJUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, throughout Canada's history, the various governments which have run this country have seeked to abolish what we call regional disparities, or at least to lessen them considerably.
When Canada came into being, it was felt that by creating a national common market, by building a railway to link east and west, not only would the economic activity be stimulated, but the wealth would be distributed more equitably between various areas. After many years, it was quickly realized that it was not sufficient to link east and west with a railway, and that other means had to be found.
After the Rowell-Sirois Commission, we came to adopt the equalization formula. It was then believed that by trying to re-establish a better balance between the provinces from the standpoint of income, it would be possible to abolish those disparities or at least to lessen them to a considerable extent.
Well, in spite of all those commendable efforts, it was quickly realized that this second method was still insufficient. Then came the series of special programs designed to assist the areas of the country which were developing less rapidly than the others.
As early as the thirties, the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, better known under the name of PFRA, was enacted. Somewhat similar legislation was in effect in the Maritimes. Then, what has been called ARDA was enacted in order to promote rural development. The ambit of ARDA was later enlarged in order to implement more general programs under FRED. Then we attempted, with industrial incentives, to encourage the establishment of industries in areas with a slower rate of growth.
Last year, on July 1st I think, the House passed a new piece of legislation on industrial incentives which provided for the setting up of special areas and gave us the authority to help those individuals faced with readjustment problems because we realized that up to that point, in spite of our efforts, disparities remained.
Had these programs not been applied, would these disparities be the same? We can safely say that they would probably be greater than they are now. However, these are hypothetical inferences which make it rather difficult to reach concrete conclusions.
When we initiated these new programs, we did not kid ourselves. We never though that overnight we would succeed in solving the problem of regional disparities in Canada. On the contrary we knew we would have to spend quite some time on it.

November 19, 1970

For instance, when a subsidy is granted to a company, normally it takes one or two years before that company goes into production, especially if it is of a certain size.
The same situation applies to special areas where we undertook the develop an infrastructure in order to create development centres capable of providing the various areas of Canada with equal opportunities. We know fully well that the designation of an area is not enough to solve its problems but the tools needed to give equal opportunities to Canadians, wherever they live, are available to us.
A moment ago I was reading the speech made yesterday by the member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas). He said of course-that is his usual argument-that not only did the government fail to do anything to eliminate regional disparities but that they have increased since this government is in power.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make my first remark now. The slate of programs I administer have never been designed to fight a general economic slow-down in this country. These regional development programs can reach their full efficiency provided the overall economy works normally. Therefore neither ARDA nor FRED nor the law on industrial incentives should be expected to straighten up our entire economy. We should rather consider these measures under their true aspects.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, part of it refers to the previous regional industrial incentives program, and part of it to the new legislation.
The 774 plants I have mentioned are not all in operation now; however they should be before long and this will provide jobs, as I said.
Concerning the other programs applying to special areas-ARDA, FRED, PFRA and so forth-I can say that they led to the creation of new jobs and to the investment of large amounts of money. In fact, in the Atlantic provinces, $167.6 million have been invested and 10,060 jobs have been created. In the province of Quebec, $40.6 million have been invested and 2,550 jobs have been created. In Ontario, $5.5 million were invested and 330 jobs were created. In western Canada, $31.2 million were invested and 1,870 jobs were created. Total outlays amount to $246 million and new jobs number 14,810. If one takes into account the number of jobs indirectly created, the total figure is about 34,000 new jobs.
Obviously this alone is not sufficient to solve the general unemployment problem in Canada. But to say that our programs designed to minimize regional disparities have not been and are not operative, is sheer irresponsibility. These programs are working well and we are enjoying very valuable co-operation from the Maritime provinces, from Quebec as well as from the other provinces. Furthermore we have reasons to believe that if these programs are intensified, they will help in substantially

reducing the disparities that have existed ever since Confederation.
Once again I say, Mr. Speaker, that those programs are not intended to restore a general situation which is unsatisfactory and which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) has dealt with to some considerable length indicating the solutions he wanted to propose. I feel that these regional expansion programs are very thorough. There are others, for instance, the relocation plans in Newfoundland, and the "New Start", program which results in extremely interesting experiments. I believe that all this is worthwhile and that one must not expect from it what can be achieved through a fiscal or general policy aimed at achieving full employment in Canada.
I do not intend to repeat the speech delivered by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson). There are, obviously, reasons for inflation; but I shall merely comment on these. This government should not have to make a choice between inflation and unemployment. Ours is a matter of finding out whether inflation is going to create more unemployment than the anti-inflation steps that we have taken.
Now, if we had to do this over again, would we proceed in the same way? I am far from sure, Mr. Speaker. It could be that a more stringent policy would be required with regard to prices, profits and salaries. At the present time, some balance is being re-established, and, with the help of the measures we will be taking shortly, I believe that we shall succeed in creating a dynamic economy, one in which Canadians will feel happy.
However, my department should not be asked to work miracles, we are unable to do so. We have already accomplished much, and I am not including here a number of measures in the regional field for which I claim neither merit nor glory. I could mention, for instance, Devco in Nova Scotia. Also, thanks to the former Atlantic Development Board, known as ADB, sustained efforts have been made. I am sure that, without such undertakings, disparities would be even worse than they are now.
Mr. Speaker, I simply and strongly challenge the hon. member's comments to which I referred a while ago. Instead of downgrading all the efforts made jointly by the provincial, federal and often local authorities, we should appreciate these worthwhile programs. Of course, we should not expect from them more than they can normally give.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED LACK OF POLICIES AND PROGRAMS TO PREVENT UNEMPLOYMENT, POVERTY AND SOCIAL INJUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) brought forward the following motion, and I quote:
That this House condemns the government for increasing the economic inequalities between different regions of Canada by its opposition to full employment policy and its refusal to use short term and long term programs in a timely and effective manner to prevent the resulting recession-level poverty and social injustice now widespread in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, taking into consideration facts as they are, one cannot but agree with the Leader of the Opposition and say he was quite justified in introducing a motion of non-confidence toward the present government.
During the new minutes available to me, Mr. Speaker,
I would like to make a rapid review of the economic situation of the province of Quebec.
Surely, no one will blame me for pointing out the weaknesses in the province of Quebec. I do so, hoping to help the people in power to do away with the disparities from which stems the growing unrest in my province.
Quebec has the largest number of unemployed in Canada. From September 1965 to September 1970, Quebec accounted for between 27.5 to 28 per cent of the national labour force, while the rate of unemployment, compared with the national figure, ranged between 35.5 and 41.5 per cent. Except for the Maritime provinces, over the last ten years the rate of unemployment has always been higher in Quebec than in the other provinces.
Mr. Speaker, I am not saying that those who have more than we do, in the province of Quebec, should be penalized in order to improve our lot. I think the Mari-times also deserve special attention, since their economic situation is very unsatisfactory.
I am sorry to say that in October 1970, 8.8 per cent of the labour force in Quebec was unemployed. In fact, the percentage was higher because the statistics provided exclude workers on retraining allowances. Therefore, it is certain that there are more than 159,000 unemployed in the province of Quebec, including those who get unemployment or retraining allowances.
The Quebec labour force is increasing more rapidly than the employment opportunities. Between 1961 and 1969, the Quebec labour force increased by 25 per cent; during the same period, jobs increased only by 17 per cent.
We therefore note a gap between the number of workers and the anticipated number of jobs. Young Quebecers especially are affected by unemployment. The unemployment rate among young Quebecers from 14 to 24 years of age reaches 11 per cent. This rate is much too high when we want to keep people happy and confident in their future and we must absolutely enable them to earn a decent living.
There is a large percentage of chronic unemployment in the province of Quebec. Indeed, 28 per cent of claims from that provinces as of August 31, 1970 covered a period of at least 27 weeks. In addition, a survey of the chronic unemployed in Canada shows that Quebec has 31 per cent of claimants and that claims extend to more than 27 weeks.
A considerable number of unemployed reside also in the Montreal area and it is essential that some steps be immediately taken to check that national evil which is unemployment. It has been proved that 40 per cent of the unemployed people of Quebec who receive unemployment insurance benefits are from Montreal.

November 19, 1970

What is the situation in the business world? More than half of commercial bankruptcies in Canada have been registered in Quebec. In other words, the province of Quebec is lagging behind in both industry and labour. The government has much to do in order to cope with the situation.
In 1969, 52 per cent of Canadian bankruptcies were recorded in the province of Quebec. Several sectors of the Quebec industry have suffered from some decline during 1970, but on the other hand, in certain other industries, some encouraging signs have to be noted. It is to be hoped that the situation will keep improving so that our industries may offer more and more jobs to Canadian people who need them.
About 30 per cent of the new manufacturing plants were established in the province of Quebec between 1960 and 1969, mostly between 1960 and 1964 rather than between 1965 and 1969.
In the field of home building, the situation is far less than comforting in Canada, particularly in the province of Quebec. During 1970, home starts declined in this province as compared with the previous year. There is a shortage of housing, because when families want to put a roof over their heads, they have much difficulty in finding one.
In 1961, 17,204 homes were built in Montreal, 17,518 in Toronto. In 1969, 23,650 homes were built in Montreal and 31,874 in Toronto, which is an increase of 81.9 per cent for Toronto and only 37.5 per cent for Montreal during the same period. During the first nine months of 1970, the situation in Montreal did not improve greatly.
What do we see now as far as prices and costs are concerned, Mr. Speaker? The price that consumers have to pay in Montreal for some commodities and services is substantially higher than in the other regions of Canada. For its bonds the government of the province of Quebec has to grant a much higher interest rate than any other provincial government. Ontario grants an interest rate of 6.85 and 8.84 per cent for its bonds if they are held to maturity. Quebec rates range from 9 to 9.6 per cent for similar securities.
Let us have a look at the current situation in the field of investments. There is a disastrous disparity between Ontario and Quebec as far as job-creating investments are concerned.
Total investments scheduled in Quebec for 1970 amount to 3 billion 400 million dollars compared with 7 billion 100 million dollars in Ontario. Quebec whose population represents only four fifths of that of Ontario receives only half as much investment as Ontario does.
Despite the fact that its population represents 29 per cent of that of the whole of Canada, the province of Quebec is getting a mere 19 per cent of the total Canadian investments. Six years ago investments in Quebec amounted to approximately 75 per cent of what Ontario was getting and to somehwere around 26 per cent of the Canadian total.
Employment Programs
During the last few years, capital investments dwindled in practically all areas except one and present forecasts are none too bright.
Personal income which is of interest to us all, has decreased in the province of Quebec.
The average hourly rate is lower in Quebec than in British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba and Ontario but higher than in the Maritimes and Saskatchewan.
Wages paid in industries in Quebec are generally lower than those paid in other regions of the country, except the Maritimes.
Personal per capita income has been constantly lower m Quebec than in all other provinces except the Maritimes. However, some improvement is noted in the situation in Quebec.
In my opinion, this short review of economic conditions in the province of Quebec shows beyond doubt that a situation exists in this province which it is urgent to correct as soon as possible.
The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) described a few moments ago the work which has been done by his department during the last few months. I agree with him that his department has made a tremendous effort to try to correct the situation, but because of the steps taken by his government to fight inflation, unemployment has increased, bringing about even more poverty among the people. I am certainly one who would wish his department were more successful but I am afraid that with some of the projects suggested by the minister we will, within a few years, be facing situations not too encouraging.
Some of our cities' small and middle-sized industries would certainly deserve assistance from the minister's department in the form of loans. They do not solicit grants unnecessarily, being convinced they can be selfsufficient. If these industries could get interesting loans at latively low interest rates, they could go on offering employment to many Canadians, this to the benefit of all.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED LACK OF POLICIES AND PROGRAMS TO PREVENT UNEMPLOYMENT, POVERTY AND SOCIAL INJUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House at the present time states, in essence, that the government is not making the economic system work. There are, of course, many people who will agree with that statement. The amendment moved by my leader, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), suggests that there is a lack of defined purpose in the government's programs and that its efforts are essentially not being adequately directed to meeting the wellbeing of people across Canada. I am glad that hon. members have an opportunity, through this amendment and motion, to discuss the government's regional development policies in particular. I suggest that the government's performance in tackling regional development and poverty problems has become a national disgrace. The government has failed to even make a start in its so-called war on poverty. All of us will acknowledge quite freely that some good things have been done, but the show that the government has put on in respect of these programs has been nothing more than a sham and a farce.
* (4:00 p.m.)
There are some 4 million to 5 million Canadians living in a state of poverty today, and another 3 million or so in varying states of deprivation. I suggest that the federal government had better realize there is a different mood and attitude toward conditions of poverty and hardship today. People are not prepared to tolerate unsatisfactory conditions indefinitely because they know they do not have to be that way, and they know that many of the disparities which exist are due to various elements of exploitation in both the present and the past.
The government has faced serious problems in the province of Quebec over the past month and a half. If the government had shown as much concern with tackling
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Laniel) .1
basic economic and social problems in Quebec as it is now showing in tracking down elusive bands of criminal conspirators and adventurers, it would never have been faced with some of the problems now before us. I was particularly struck by some excerpts I read recently from a book written, but not yet published, by Pierre Val-lieres, one of the people now held on charges in Montreal. This book entitled "White Niggers of America" describes his view of the Quebec society in which he grew up. No doubt all of us will have disagreements with some of the views expressed, but we ignore them at our peril.
I noted one excerpt in which he described the conditions in which his family lived in Ville Jacques-Cartier, a community on the south shore of the St. Lawrence across from Montreal. It reads as follows:
The shack was made of wood covered with "papier brique", a kind of tarpaper designed to look like brick. In the centre front was a little white porch. Inside, only three rooms: in the middle a kitchen, which also served as dining room, living room, bath room, etc., to the left, a large bedroom which my parents shared with Raymond (who was not yet walking); lastly, to the right, a tiny room with a double-decker bed and a chest of drawers, this was the room of "the two oldest", Andre and me. The rooms were separated by walls of "donnaconna", a kind of hard, thick cardboard which could be bought quite cheaply from any dealer in building materials. Manufactured by Domtar in the Portneuf region (I think), "donnaconna" was easy to cut up, install and paint, and it was usually sold in panels four feet by eight. Many of the shacks that went up in Ville Jacques-Cartier in the years following our arrival were built entirely out of two-by-fours and broad panels of this economical cardboard, which was then covered with tarpaper. It was not exactly warm in the winter, but it didn't cost much, and with this miraculous material you could build a little house in two days!
Our shack seemed almost luxurious compared to most of the hovels in Longueuil-Annexe, which were covered with black tarpaper and looked like sinister old shanties abandoned in a swamp. On rainy days especially, Longueuil-Annexe looked like a burnt-out shantytown. The only trouble with this shantytown was that it was inhabited, to adopt the phrase of the Quebecois poet Roland Giguere.
This excerpt struck me forcefully because it reflected the viewpoint of one who had given up hope of being able to make meaningful change or improvements in society through existing institutions. That is a bad situation. As I read this excerpt, I thought of similar conditions I have seen in the past in Saskatchewan and, indeed, other parts of Canada. Fortunately, there was a difference. In my own province people did not give up hope. That was the great accomplishment of people like M. J. Coldwell, T. C. Douglas and others who led a new political movement in Saskatchewan in the 1930's. They offered hope of meaningful change, improvement and a better life through the democratic process. People felt there was a way out of their dilemma. For some today in Canada, for whatever reason, that hope does not exist. But the government says: Look at all the money we are spending. True, there is a lot of money being spent as the minister indicated this afternoon but the question is, how is the money being spent and is it doing the job.
My leader, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), pointed out yesterday that to the end of 1969 $46,176,000 in grants was provided to United States corporations by the Department of Region-
November 19, 1970

al Economic Expansion while only $20,877,000 was made available to Canadian concerns. Surely, this policy is in serious conflict with any attempt that might be made to check the growing influence of foreign corporations in Canada.
Let me refer to another matter. Yesterday my leader drew attention to an answer given to me this week that some $95,500,000 in grants have been made available by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion which will provide 17,284 jobs. This makes only a very small dent in the unemployment situation. It might be worth noting that many of these jobs are not yet in existence. It is true the government has made a commitment to assist Canadian concerns, but the government I suggest is making many of these grants in an ad hoc fashion. They assist a variety of operators but whether the benefits envisaged will be achieved is not at all certain. I can give one example which came to my attention recently. It concerns my home town where I grew up, the town of Humboldt, which is in the consituency of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Lang).
Last June an announcement was made that $512,000 was to be provided for a poultry processing plant that cost some $1,200,000 and would provide about 207 jobs. I find that this company does not yet have the land on which to put up that plant. It has taken out an option but does not really, as yet, own the land that is available to it. The company is trying to raise capital. It has the $500,000 grant, or the commitment for it, and now is trying to raise the rest of the capital amount ng to $800,000. I presume this would include some provision for working capital as well as the capital cost of the plant.
Apparently the company has some $370,000 or so now which it raised through a farm grain deal that ties in with other operations of the company, namely, some feed mill operations. I am subject to correction on this point, but the information I have at the moment suggests that the principals involved in this particular operation will not have to put up one penny of their own money. Certainly, that will be the case if this company is successful in raising the $800,000 in capital it is trying to raise in the district before construction of the plant can be commenced.
I don't want to suggest that I do not want to see a plant of this sort in my old home town, even though it is not in my constituency at the present time, but certainly I feel we need to look at these proposed operations with a view to seeing that they are efficient and, are developed in a manner which will be to the benefit of the communities concerned.
I suggest that the government is engaging in the worst type of "ad hocery" in its regional development programs. Where is the concern for the impact of these programs or how they meet the needs of the community?
I suggest plants must meet adequate tests before they are started, regardless of the incentive. Until it has been shown that these proposed plants can meet adequate tests in respect of economic criteria and that they will be viable operations, the government should not throw away money on operators of various types, friends of the gov-
Employment Programs
ernment and foreign interests. The government is not planning or providing the type of framework that is needed in this regard. I suggest that it does have to grapple with the needs of the total economy, and I suggest it has not done this to date. This, of course, is essential if regional development programs are to be successful.
In this regard, I agree with the minister that two aspects of the situation have to be co-ordinated. The government is not adequately tackling the total problems in respect of the economy. The prices and incomes approach-the Boy Scout approach-has been a failure. The government has not developed an economic policy which would help to deal with the disparities that exist in this country. It certainly has not moved toward full employment. Four hundred and nineteen thousand people are out of work at the present time; some 9 per cent to 11 per cent of the labour force may be out of work before the winter is over. Regional development programs must be planned and the planners must take a long run approach. These programs must also be geared to time considerations and to the needs that exist at present. I suggest that further attention must be given to the whole question of providing an adequate infrastructure for the communities concerned, and efforts must be made to develop it. Rural problems must be tackled. The Indian and Metis peoples' problems must be tackled. The government must avoid pitfalls and must beware of the growth of situations leading to the types of comments that have been made by some people in this country recently. The government should remember the words of some of the people who are now taking a very bitter attitude toward our country.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I suggest that the government should place high priority on regional development programs and on correcting regional inequalities. To date its programs have been a failure. It is late in the day, but the government must correct its course while there is still time.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED LACK OF POLICIES AND PROGRAMS TO PREVENT UNEMPLOYMENT, POVERTY AND SOCIAL INJUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion now under consideration is one of those which makes us look back to live once more what we generally call the "good old days."
A world war ended in 1945, 25 years ago already, and our country went from full employment to a state of deplorable conditions where unemployment ranges from five to 12 per cent depending on the areas. Should we come to the conclusion that wartime is necessary to create full employment? Is it true that these would be the only possible conclusions for our narrow minds?
I should like to suggest to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Lang) and to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) that they take retraining lessons from the masters of work and labour in Germany which we destroyed so completely during World War II and which today stands as a model to the whole world, as far as full employment is concerned.

November 19, 1970
Employment Programs
On November 11, 1970, the official day set aside to honour the memory of our dead soldiers of the last two world wars, La Presse, the Montreal newspaper, published an article on the progress of automation in Germany where there is work for everyone. This is quite enlightening and impressive.
On page 3 of section "J" of the November 11 issue of La Presse, one can read the following:
During these last ten years, automation and rationalization have "freed" 13 million workers in West Germany. Yet, they have not become unemployed: with a few exceptions, they did not even have to learn a new trade.
__the workers, the government and the unions nevertheless
follow closely the development of the employment market, because they still remember the great world economic crisis of 1929-30 with its devastating consequences in the domestic field.
Even if the whole article is interesting to read, I will quote but the last paragraph:
There is no need therefore to be pessimistic for 1980: the number of vacancies will always be greater than that of jobs wanted.
That is simply marvelous and that is happening in capitalist Germany, under the eyes of our capitalist country. In 1970, we even get large loans from that country in order to finance our administrative deficiencies in Canada, and particularly in the province of Quebec.
If Germany can thus export capital, and at the same time maintain full employment on its own territory, why not also ask that country to export its experts in full employment, whom we could put at the head of our departments to replace inefficient nrnisters, who can only preach resignation in the face of our own inertness in filling the vacuum of a sick administration suffering from incurable unconcern.
Mr. Speaker, this happy situation of labour in Germany is due, and I quote:
-to the necessary qualifications, to the permanent training and to the sensible direction given to the growing generation-
The whole policy in the field of education is geared to the future by taking into account the high requirements of productivity for the next decade. This is enough, I believe, to shake us awake. These objectives are achievable since they have already been attained by men in Germany.
It is just possible, in my view, that men living in Canada achieve a similar aim. I urge that a mission of our most insignificant officials in charge of full employment be sent to Germany to undergo a conclusive retraining which would be profitable to the hard-working Canadian people who, as a whole, have always been willing to do their best under the leadership of their elite.
Let us not kid ourselves: the misgivings of a people always come as a result of the misgivings of its leaders. When a bus overturns, the fault does not lie with the passengers who bought their tickets. Let us rather look for the driver.
In Canada, we have everything we need except goodwill among our leadership.
When an economic problem such as unemployment arises, why not seek first its causes? Let us stop making speeches, ordering inquiries, issuing white papers.
If we are really unable to find out who is at fault, this merely means that we are unwilling to suppress unemployment.
Unemployment, inflation, poverty, excessive taxation, these are many economic ills that cannot be said to derive from earthquakes, tidal waves, floods or acts of God. No, those ills derive from the action of our statesmen and financial leaders.
We are being governed by inefficient and blind people. "Can the blind lead the blind? Both shall fall into the ditch." This is written in the Gospel. The Bible says also: "The light of the body is the eye: therefore, when thine eye is single, thy whole body also is full of light."
If, as in Germany, management is enlightened, the whole labour force benefits from it. There is no unemployment, no inflation in that country. Probably their fiscal and financial system is adequate to the size of a productivity commensurate with their population and their natural resources.
All these things we have in abundance in Canada, but we lack adequate leadership. It must be realized, understood and stated in order to change the situation.
Let us replace the incompetent leaders, not only in the labour field, but in the areas of finance, currency, politics, industry and university training.
If our elite fails us, if our institutions are inefficient, let us proceed to the necessary changes and we will achieve our purposes.
Our whole administrative, monetary, economic and political activities overlook the real objectives and only seek profit. At the present time, this is where the trouble lies. We seek financial gain rather than satisfy the citizens' needs.
That is why in a period of unemployment, labour is sacrificed to financial profit.
That is why, even in war-time, life is sacrificed while finance reaps profits. In times of inflation, the cost of living goes up, taxes are increased, and all the citizens suffer. But finance pays off. Interest rates go up even as high as 10 and 12 per cent, but finance still makes profits.
What do we do when there is unemployment? We study its causes and show how it can be checked. But if we do not want to check it, then nothing can be done. The government could put an end to unemployment overnight, for they have the means to do so.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) himself knows what to do, but he will not do it. He has the means to force his ministers to do away with unemployment, but he does not want to use them to that end.
It is inconceivable that unemployment should be tolerated. Fortunately, there is one remedy that can be applied at once to stimulate purchases by making more money available to consumers.

November 19, 1970

Who wrote this important sentence? None other than the present Prime Minister, on page 33 of the March 1954 issue of Cite Libre, under the title "Fluctuations econo-miques et methodes de stabilisation", and I quote:
Competition among producers would result in price reductions. Competition among the unemployed seeking a job would bring about lower wages, which would reduce production costs. The interest rate would decline accordingly, and new investments would thus become profitable. Hut today, prices and wages are prevented from going down by monopolies and labour unions.
Here is what the author said on page 34 of the same issue:
The problem is still to find out whether there is any other limit to unemployment than utter destitution.
The most obvious solution would be to equalize the incomes among the various social classes, so that the poor would have more money to spend, the rich less to save.
The following is found on page 35:
The government will then be compelled to increase its expenditures (railways, roads, airports, parks). As long as such needs exist, it is inconceivable that unemployment should be tolerated.
Fortunately, there is one remedy that can be applied at once -to stimulate purchases by making more money available to consumers. The state must distribute largely and determinedly all kinds of allowances-
Mr. Speaker, I shall quote a few excerpts from the March 1954 issue of Cite Libre:
-to stimulate purchases by making more money available to consumers.
This is what the Prime Minister was then advocating. Today, now that he has been elected thanks to an election fund supported by high finance, he merely reverses his opinions. Consumers are not only neglected, but he even asks them their co-operation by requiring them to tighten their belt.
The Creditistes have demanded that the purchasing power be distributed well before 1954 and they are still demanding it.
We are demanding it, because we already have the products and unfortunately, there are also needy costumers.
Among those who are expecting higher benefits are veterans, widows, needy mothers, disabled persons, father and mothers who are asking for increased family allowances, the unemployed, permanent or seasonal, and all workers who are paid a salary they consider inadequate to meet their commitments. As the present Prime Minister once stated, and I quote:
The state must distribute largely and determinedly all kinds of allowances-
Then, why not pay a salary to students? How many students are now facing financial problems? Why maintain and defend the system which is causing concern to them?
Mr. Speaker, these are so many reasons why it is urgent to implement the measures advocated in 1954 by our present Prime Minister.
Employment Programs
Since American economists and sociologists have stated in a open letter to President Johnson that the first condition to avoid economical and social troubles, in the present state of production, is to ensure that each individual and each family is guaranteed a minimum income as a right, let me repeat the famous statement of the Prime Minister, and I quote:
"The state should distribute profusely and resolutely all kinds of allowances so as to stimulate consumption."
This sentence is all the more true today because, since 1954, the value of our national production has increased from only 25 billion to an expected 80 billion in 1970.
Mr. Speaker, I feel quite at ease to suggest that this type of administration be tried since, as early as 1954, the right hon. Prime Minister declared: "Fortunately, this remedy can be administered right now."
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED LACK OF POLICIES AND PROGRAMS TO PREVENT UNEMPLOYMENT, POVERTY AND SOCIAL INJUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the appropriateness of this motion could not be any more heavily underlined than by the headline in yesterday's Toronto Star reading, "Unemployment Rate for Last 3 Months Worst in 25 Years." Since there was virtually no unemployment during the war, this means it is the highest it has been since the dirty 30's. The article goes on to say that there were 140,000 more Canadians looking for jobs in the last three months of this year than last year, representing the highest third-quarter unemployment rate since World War II.
Canada's economic progress faces an uncertain future. At the moment Canada's surplus export sales are at a record of $2,250,000,000 for the first ten months, up from $561 million in 1969. Purchases from the United States have continued to drop, while our sales to them have continued to increase. There is good evidence that this state of affairs may not continue, but rather be reversed. In so far as our automotive trade is concerned, it has turned out to be one of the brightest spots in our over-all trade, but not because of particularly good management but rather as a result of a fluke that a particular small car was very popular. The automotive pact is under heavy attack in the United States because there is great pressure to bring automobile production back home. President Nixon contends that because of the protection afforded Canada, undue pressure is on his government to have the pact abolished.
There is a rising protectionist movement in the United States and our ministers have been warning them about it. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) has stated that growth in Canadian manufacturing is necessary to improve job opportunities. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin), in a speech delivered in the United States, has just reiterated this sentiment. To illustrate how this protectionist sentiment is rising, Phillips Electronics Industries Ltd. of Toronto recently decided to bid on supplying Chrysler Corporation of Detroit with car radios. Chrysler placed the order in Detroit, and an official of that company said strong political pressure in the United States had caused the order to be shifted

November 19, 1970
Employment Programs
because it was felt that the auto agreement was working too much in favour of Canada. It is believed that this switch will result in 700 people being laid-off.
Then, Eaton Automotive announced on November 16, the closing of its London division early next year because the products made by the London plant are now being made in the U.S.A. This company is likely also under political pressure to maintain employment in their factories in the United States. Surely, this is a lesson for the strong nationalists who think we can live completely alone. We have the textile industry in chronic trouble as a result of low-priced imports, and the government is to amend the Export-Import Act to allow it to set mandatory import quotas. This is our own form of protection, yet we lament others raising their tariffs.
Then, there is the very probable entry of the United Kingdom into the European Common Market. It seems very probable that there will be a serious loss of markets, and especially could this be so in agricultural exports. The European Common Market is showing considerable protectionist tendencies.
Again, Mr. Speaker, the United States is suffering from a recession just as Canada is. It would seem likely that multi-national companies of both countries will be expected to expand in the United States. If the nationalism that is now so rampant in Canada against all things American continues, then those companies are most likely to consider themselves unwelcome in Canada. The Premier of Quebec has been telling Americans that they can only come to Quebec if they speak French, in effect telling them that they can only come in under severe restriction.
The Canadian economy is moving into a hard winter, largely as a result of Canadian government policies. It takes time for fiscal and monetary controls to take effect because such changes, either inflationary or deflationary, take time to work. The brakes applied a year ago are only beginning to take effect now, a year later. Similarly, the switch of the government to deficit financing, and the large expansion of the money supply, will not show up until next year. Even with these brakes applied, the price increase has still been running at 3 per cent, which is still very high. We should not forget that the Canadian economy is mainly supported by our great export industries. Without the great export boom, the nation would be in serious economic difficulties indeed. The outlook for profits in all but a few fortunately placed industries is much reduced, as is the outlook for the capital investment necessary to create new jobs and reduce unemployment.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
The Prime Minister himself on the CBC program "Encounter," being interviewed by Charles Lynch on November 5, stated:
We have been homing in on unemployment in Quebec and in the Maritimes because this is where unemployment is highest, and we've done so by pouring in literally hundreds of millions of dollars in the past few years into those areas through regional economic expansion. Other hundreds of millions of dollars more through manpower retraining programs. Just a month or two ago another hundred million dollars for housing.

Now, Mr. Speaker, it is quite obvious that much of these hundreds of millions of dollars that have been poured into regional economic expansion in Quebec have not been as effective as they should have been. I think we all realize that much of the money spent in regional economic expansion must at best be considered a social expenditure and not recoverable in the form of economic gains. This great debate will have to come some time in the future.
I would like now to turn to what I feel is an important factor in our current economic trouble and that is the freeing of the Canadian dollar last May. For the second time since the end of the Second World War Canada removed, on May 31, the fixed rate of exchange of its dollar. In both cases, the rise took place under a Liberal government when the United States was engaged in a limited war. The response to the inflow of American capital resulting from the Korean War was the floating of the exchange rate 20 years ago.
This year the decision to abandon the fixed value appeared less urgent, particularly if proper precautions had been taken. The Canadian economy was not drawing in funds for expansion but was able to remain stable only because of a temporary surge of exports to western Europe and Japan, along with auto exports to the United States. The domestic side of the Canadian economy exhibited sagging tendencies. In the first six months of 1970, the merchandise trade surplus reached $1,246 million compared to $208 million in 1969. However, there does not appear to be much special life to exports and United States trade policy appears to be on the verge of becoming more protectionist, tending to depress exports to that country.
The huge merchandise trade balance was the result of several non-recurring factors. Demand for Canadian base metals received special stimulus after the strikes last year. Automobile exports, which alone accounted for 20 per cent of the gain in exports, benefitted from the popularity of a particular small car manufactured in Canada, but later this year several competitive models will be built in the United States, so that this can be regarded as a non-recurring event. Metal prices are declining most noticeably on the volatile London Metal Exchange, and shipments to the United States will decline because capital spending is very metal intensive, and as capital spending declines, metal shipments will also experience less buoyant markets.
Defence sharing agreements which have led to a spillover to companies such as Canadair will no longer be a favourable trade factor for Canada; even though, in all likelihood, the war will continue, more defence production will be handled in relatively depressed United States areas like southern California. In 1968 United States defence spending in Canada amounted to $320 million, in 1969 $300 million and 1970 will probably be lower. Because of balance of payments problems in the United States, direct investment in Canada will be discouraged. It is scheduled to drop from $2.67 billion in 1970 to $2.18 billion in 1972. Oil shipments may also suffer a temporary decline.
November 19, 1970

The relative strength of the Canadian dollar depends on our merchandise trade balance and the flow of the capital account. The latter is affected by, first, short term inflows, usually as a result of a difference in interest rates, or the desire for an alternative haven by investors concerned about their own country; second, long term inflows which stem from either direct investment, nonresident purchases of securities, or borrowing outside of Canada by government or corporations. Hitherto changes in the relative values of the Canadian dollar reflected short term inflows; that is, changes in foreign holdings of Canadian currency and foreign assets of Canadian chartered banks.
This summer the short term inflow stemmed not from a relatively alluring spread of interest between Canada and the United States, but from the unusually large merchandise trade balance and the repatriation of short term funds. The funds returned to Canada after the white paper on taxation proposed that investment and capital gains in non-Canadian securities would be penalized. The applicable provisions would restrict to 10 per cent the percentage of pensions fund assets that could be held in non-Canadian investments and capital gains in non-Canad an investment would attract a 50 per cent capital gains tax compared to a 25 per cent capital gains tax on widely held Canad:an investments. This is another example of the way in which the white paper on taxation materially increased the pressure on the Canadian dollar with an untoward and unexpected affect, even though no change in the law has taken place up to now.
Furthermore, the Quebec election gave some renewed confidence to lure investment back to Canada after the panic exodus earlier this year. Much too little was done to counterbalance these factors. The Minister of Finance foolishly chose to ignore these trends. Foreign exchange reserves improved by $267 million in the first quarter of 1970. In April reserves were increased by an additional $225 million. Canada, however, should be carrying higher exchange reserves on average than it did during the decade of the previous fluctuating rate. This is not the case. If strong counterbalancing efforts had been made earlier this year, short term inflows could have been checked, temporarily at least.
One reason often cited for the revaluation of the Canadian dollar is our relatively better control over inflation. The "state of the art" is such that it is doubtful that price movements can be measured with any such precision but even if Canada maintained greater price stability over the last year or two, this, even in combination with our large merchandise trade balance, did not warrant an unpegging of the dollar.
A common argument against a fixed rate of exchange is that it leads to alterations in monetary and fiscal policy for exchange reasons rather than to promote a satisfactory level of domestic income employment and growth. However, this summer concurrently with and because of the abandonment of the system of fixed exchange, the Minister of Finance announced an easier money policy. This was implied by the Bank of Canada's reduction in bank rate from 7.5 per cent to 7 per cent. The reduction
Employment Programs
in interest rates can be expected to reduce the incentive for short term funds to flow into Canada and to relieve the upward pressure in the dollar. The Minister of Finance thus was acting to have fiscal and monetary policy influence the exchange rate; proponents of a floating rate have claimed that this was like having the tail wag the dog. Interest rate differentials with 1he United States are now narrower than usual. If such an easy monetary policy had been adopted in March when the United States federal reserve board indicated it was moving toward easier money, (he upward speculative push on the Canadian dollar in all likelihood would have been avoided. However, all winter and spring the Bank of Canada and the Department of Finance adhered to a relatively restrictive course in order to arrest inflationary pressures.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I notice that the motion before the House refers to long term programs to cure unemployment. I am glad it contains that language because some of the suggestions I wish to make relate to a long term cure for unemployment. I am also glad that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) is in the House. I wish to talk briefly about atomic energy plants and the part they could play in this long term cure.
Since unemployment is not caused by one factor solely, the cure for unemployment also will not involve merely one factor. We must do a great many things if we wish to cure unemployment. I should like to talk for a few moments about some ideas I have for this long term cure.
This morning in committee I asked the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) how our money is being spent on research. The point of my question was this: I felt that we were adopting a scattered approach in our spending on research, and that we ought to concentrate. Since we do not have enough money to spend on all areas of research, we ought to concentrate on those areas that will be of greatest advantage to us. We ought to concentrate consciously on those areas of research in which we can compete with other countries effectively. We must concentrate on those resources and goods with which we can compete with other countries of the world. As I say, we cannot afford to indulge in research in all areas, so we had better specialize.
A few weeks ago I visited the atomic energy plant at Gentilly, Quebec, and I must say I was surprised at what is being done there. I regret that we have not sold plants of this type abroad. It seems to me that the government has been somewhat remiss in the amount of money it has devoted to this particular type of development. We seem to be developing a type of atomic energy plant that is different from atomic energy plants elsewhere. I am not saying this is wrong. Hopefully, this may have been a wise move. It may have been the best thing to do. Yet, benefits do not come about automatically. We must be
1332

I have visited the CBC station in Ottawa, a radar base in my constituency, the Atomic Energy plant at Gentilly and, as a member of the Standing Committee on Agriculture, some food processing plants. A great deal of the industrial equipment used in all these plants is manufactured in foreign countries. I am not knocking these other countries because they are able to produce this equipment cheaply and effectively so that it is economic for us to purchase it. However, I feel that some of this equipment could be produced just as well in Canada.
The electronics industry is too small and fragmented to compete with foreign firms. Possibly the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce could give some leadership to rationalizing this field so that more of this equipment could be produced in Canada. I do not think it would be economically feasible to produce all of this equipment in Canada because of our limited requirements, but some of it could be produced in this country. The government should study seriously what could be done in this respect. The government should give assistance for research, capital or whatever else is required for specified areas, so that Canadian firms will be competitive. This, in part, will solve the unemployment problem.

He made no reference to the difficulties, indeed the impossibility, of carrying out effective programs to deal with regional disparity when the fiscal and monetary policies of the government do not take into account the regional facts of life in this country.
