speechtext:
We expected the minister to make some reference to that in his speech. He is responsible to Parliament and the country for coping with these very serious problems. However, he said nothing about that. When we have occasion to raise the problems of unemployment and lack of government action in dealing with unemployment and regional disparity, the members of the government always conveniently refer to the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and the regional economic programs which are supposed to be the be-all and end-all.
We must examine these programs for their effectiveness in coping with unemployment and regional disparity. We must examine them in the context of growing unemployment. Today's unemployment is the most serious for this period since the depression of the 1930's. This is evidenced by the latest Dominion Bureau of Statistics' figures. We must look at the programs under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, we must look at them in that context.
The main thrust of the government's regional development policy is the Regional Development Incentives Act. Yesterday I directed a question to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion. It was prompted by the tabling of figures under the Regional Development Incentives Act for the period ending October, 1970 which showed great disparities in the allocation of funds and the estimation of jobs created. For example, the province of Newfoundland received $826,000, whereas the province of Quebec received almost $40 million, almost half the total funds. By skating around the question the minister, in effect, refused to answer it. He indicated he would be participating in the debate and that he would have something to say about it at that time. We sat and listened to the minister, Mr. Speaker, but he did not say anything in this regard. We are as wise as ever.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
The provision of these grants does not take into account the fact that there are five regions in this country; most important, they fail to take note of the fact that under the Regional Development Incentives Act the initiatives are in the hands of industry, not the hands of government. In my opinion this is the major weakness of this program. This illustrates the reason for the wide ranging disparities in the allocation of funds under the program. Companies obviously establish in more attractive areas where they can attain the same incentives as those provided for locating in some of the more remote parts of the country. Instead of locating in Newfoundland, or northern Saskatchewan, or northern Ontario they would obviously choose the more populous areas in Quebec around Montreal and Quebec City, or they would choose southern Ontario. This is surely the major weak-

November 19, 1970
Employment Programs
ness in the program. This is why the program should be changed and its administration and concept decentralized.
Then, there is the complementary program covering the so-called designated growth areas, the program designed to enable the federal government to move into areas of provincial jurisdiction to build up the so-called infrastructure which is supposed to attract industry. Take my own city as an example. It is one of the special areas, one of the growth areas. Under this program the federal government has announced its intention to build two high schools; it has announced it will build a new access route from the Trans-Canada Highway to the harbour in St. John's; it has announced it will provide water and sewage facilities. That is good. That is tremendous, because the city of St. John's and the various school boards could not afford to provide these schools and other amenities. The municipality is already taxed to the limit. But it is my contention that not one new job will be created. I say this because we already have, in this city, the infrastructure needed to support industry. It has been there for a hundred years, but it has not been enough to encourage industry to establish there. Why? Simply because of our geographical position in relation to the major markets of this hemisphere; because of our insularity and the consequent problems of transportation costs. All the cliches used by the minister or by any of his officials in trying to sell this program will not alter the facts which I have stated. The result is we have a program in which the government ignores these facts.
The government is unable to use the Regional Development Incentives Act in the way it was designed. It is unable to use the act as a tool to stabilize the economy and increase employment. The great weakness of the program, in my view, is that the government has lost control of it. The government finds itself unable to determine what type of industry shall locate in any particular area of the country as a consequence of its planning and investigations. This initiative is entirely in the hands of the industries concerned. If it is to be effective, this program, like the government's monetary and fiscal policies intended to combat inflation, must be decentralized. It must take into account the facts of life in this country, and these include the fact that Canada is not one homogenous unit but five different regions comprising five different economies. It is because of the government's failure to take this into account that its programs are not working, and unemployment is increasing.
It is all very well to talk about the necessity of building up infrastructures under a program which enables the government to enter areas of provincial jurisdiction, but the cold fact of the matter is that the program is a flop, the program is a total failure, and the minister's unwillingness to deal with this aspect today is proof positive of my statement, if proof were needed. I think it is fair to say that the minister's program, and government policy, have become bogged down in a quagmire of "adhocery"-a maze of ad hoc programs and ad hoc decisions. Much of the difficulty has been caused by the failure of the bureaucrats and the technocrats in the minister's department to take into account the experience

and knowledge of municipal authorities and provincial governments. There has been scarcely any consultation in connection with the planning, conception and implementing of these programs. These people go across the country and look down their bureaucratic noses at the provincial and municipal authorities as being somewhat inferior; this is certainly the case in the province from which I come.
Ask any member of this House who comes from Prince Edward Island or any other area of Canada where the department is heavily involved, and he will quickly say the same thing. The department parachutes into these areas technocrats and so-called experts for the sole purpose of carrying out the wishes of the minister's deputy minister, because nobody else knows anything about this program. It is obvious the minister knows very little about what is going on. The whole show is being run by one man only. He sends out teams of experts and they fan out all across the country-"You get in there; those local yokels don't know anything." This results in all kinds of difficulty due to lack of understanding or appreciation of local conditions. The Province of Newfoundland is a classic example. They have practically taken over the department of community and social development. We even had the chairman of the Regional Development Committee down there working during the summer-I do not know what his particular expertise consists of, but he was there; he was joined by the technocrats who are still down there. They even provided a deputy minister. Nobody on the island has any say in the implementation of the program.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is all so
very clear that what has been said by the hon. member who spoke before me is nothing less than a political speech, reeking of partisanship, in the true stereotyped fashion, and seeking merely to destroy the confidence that the people of Canada have in the government's efforts to erase any regional disparity still prevailing in Canada. However, it is generally acknowledged that these efforts already have had some effects and there is no question but that given a good amount of doggedness, the scourge of unemployment may be overcome one of these days.
On the other hand, one must realize that the federal government is not the only level of administration that is responsible for setting up new industries or creating new jobs. I believe the federal, provincial and municipal governments all have to share this responsibility. The full responsibility for this situation should not be left to one government in particular.
This will perhaps lead me to make a speech which might be described as political and partisan but I shall make it all the same.
November 19, 1970

During the sixties, especially since 1963, the government of New Brunswick took its responsibilities in this field by co-operating with the federal government. One may wonder what happened in New Brunswick during these years. Several hon. members may not be interested in what goes on in the small province of New Brunswick. But for me, it is very important and it shows the degree of quality of our administration. We made more progress during this decade than during any other period in" our history since Confederation.
A recent statistical survey of the area by the Economic Council of the Atlantic provinces shows that, in the last few years, the economy has been healthy and that, in some sectors, expansion has reached a new high.
One of those sections is that of metal mining. In 1960 there was no activity whatever in mining in New Brunswick. Since then, the Heath Steele Company which had begun operating in our area in the 1950's closed its doors.
An $11 million program has since converted this mine and the concentrator it feeds into a vital element for the economy of the Northumberland constituency, in Eastern New Brunswick. Daily production is 3,000 tons and there are 270 workers. Such accomplishment is due to federal-provincial co-operation.
On the other hand the Brunswick Mining and Smelting Company operates two mines and two concentrators thanks to a $60 million investment. It produces 8,000 tons a day and has 1,025 employees.
The Nigadoo River Company mine and concentrator are now in operation. This represents an investment of $10 million. The daily output is 1,000 tons of ore and the mine provides work for 315 people.
At the present time the Anaconda American Brass is building a copper concentrator of a 1,000-ton daily capacity which should have been in operation in September this year. It means a capital investment of $6 million providing jobs for 110 workers at the present time.
I could continue, Mr. Speaker, quoting figures to show all the improvement in the New Brunswick mining sector which is due, if I may say so again, to the co-operation between provincial and federal governments that has existed particularly since 1963 and has gained momentum in the last few years.
I could talk about expansion in the forest industry which employs a great many people; this would have been impossible without the efficient part taken by the federal government. The same applies to hydro-electric power. In this respect, the hydro-electric plant at Mac-taquac is an example that speaks for itself.
Now, members opposite are blaming the federal government for the situation prevailing at this time. As for me, I believe the official opposition should perhaps examine its own conscience and go back a little to find what it failed to do while in power, in order to avoid the situations that we now know.
Employment Programs
If I may be partisan and deal again with the province of New Brunswick, I will refer particularly to the field of education in which, during the 50's, when practically nothing was done, the only effort of the provincial government was to maintain education at such a level that only about 25 per cent of the young people who attended school were able to get a degree.
Today, of course, the situation is quite different. In vocational training only, the federal government has made an enormous contribution. Before 1960, there was not a single vocational school in New Brunswick. This was really scandalous and I am somewhat ashamed to say it. But since 1960, we have had something to be proud of. In 1961, the New Brunswick Technical Institute was opened in Moncton. Building costs reached $1.9 million.^ The required equipment for the Institute has cost $1,500,000 up until now and a new $2.4 million wing was added last year, which makes a total investment of $5,800,000 about 75 per cent of which has been paid by the federal government.
Tne St. John Technical Institute, in New Brunswick, was opened in 1963. To date, building and additions cost $2,100,000. The cost of initial and additional equipment was $1,300,000, bringing the investment in the future of the youth of New Brunswick to a total of some $3,400,000.
The Bathurst Trade School did not exist in 1960. It was inaugurated in 1963. Its cost was $1,400,000 and the school is now undergoing expansion evaluated at $1,300,000, bringing the total investment for vocational training, with the assistance of the federal government to $2,700,000.
The ndmundston Trade School, in my riding, was inaugurated in 1965 and represents an investment of some $1,700,000, in vocational training.
Another trade school in my riding is the school of Grand-Sault which has just been built, and this means an investment of more than half a million dollars
Mr. Speaker, a new government has been elected in New Brunswick a few weeks ago. I really do not know if they will give the province a better administration than the previous government. Time will tell.
I do know, however, that during the sixties, considerable growth has been recorded in the field of industrial development in that province, under the leadership of the hon. Louis J. Robichaud. Remarkable and willing cooperation has been extended by the federal government, and I sincerely hope that this co-operation will carry over into this decade. I do hope so and in my opinion, all the citizens of New Brunswick expect it. The provincial government should now show its mettle, it should come out of its shell and vigorously carry on the aggressive policy set forth and implemented by the previous government.
I am sure that the federal government will not be found wanting, because of its strong present policy.

November 19, 1970

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, most of the speakers in the debate yesterday and today have been dealing, quite understandably, with the problems of unemployment, poverty and regional disparity. I intend today in the few minutes at my disposal to deal with another subject which I submit is related. The pro-

November 19, 1970
Employment Programs
jected costs of what we are doing are so tremendous that unless we think about our programs and our objectives, and unless we begin to set national goals we will create problems for this country the result of which will be that unemployment, meeting health needs and housing needs, to mention just a few of the basic needs of the people of this country, will become insoluble.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
I want to discuss the failure of the federal government in "its policy-to take the words of the amendment to the motion put forth yesterday by the leader of our party-of opting out of its responsibility to be involved in the maintenance of national standards in health, welfare and education." It has become fashionable since the arrival in Ottawa of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) increasingly to hear the view that education is a provincial responsibility under the provisions of the BNA Act, and therefore that Ottawa ought not to be and cannot be too involved in educational problems. Mr. Speaker, whether we like it or not, we are involved and we always have been involved.
Ottawa by which I mean the federal government, is involved in the education of Indians. Ottawa is involved 100 per cent in the manpower training programs. Ottawa is involved in provincial educational programs at the elementary and secondary school levels. Every time the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Mar-chand) signs an ARDA or FRED agreement with one of the provinces, with the exception of Quebec, a major component is the reorganization, upgrading and redevelopment of the educational system of that province. Ottawa is certainly involved in the financing of university education both at the undergraduate and graduate level.
Mr. Speaker, some of our top civil servants at the federal and provincial levels have been giving thought to what has happened in education and what is likely to happen within the next ten to 15 years. They have been pointing to the dangers. Unfortunately, so far as I can tell there has been no response by anybody in the federal government to their analyses, by either the Prime Minister, the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier), who has some responsibility for educational and cultural matters, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Lang), or the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion.
I commend to hon. members a speech delivered by the director of the education division of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, Dr. Wisenthal, to the conference held at Banff in October by the Alberta Human Resources Research Commission. He points out what we all know, that there has been a tremendous increase in the number of young people attending post-secondary educational institutions, universities, community colleges, technical and vocational schools. This increase is understandable. We were remiss in these kinds of programs until the last few years and have been trying to catch up. Dr. Wisenthal documents the growth in enrolment. He points out that if one takes 1961 as the base year and puts the index figure of those attending university at 100 in that year, by 1969 the figure had risen to 250.9, an
increase of more than 2J times. He projects what will happen by 1980 if we continue in the way in which we have been going. His figure for 1980 is 581.8, an increase of almost 600 per cent.
Dr. Wisenthal goes on to analyse the enrolment figures. He points out that if you take the undergraduate university enrolment in 1961 as 121.5, by 1969 it had grown to 268.2, substantially more than double. He projects this on to 1980 and comes up with the figure of 638.4, an increase of almost sixfold from 1961 to 1980. At the graduate level, and I am not too critical of this because our graduate students have traditionally gone first to Great Britain and in more recent years to the United States, he points out that where there were 7.3 thousand students doing graduate work in 1961, this figure had grown by 1969 to 30.2 thousand, and by 1980 he estimates it will grow to 111.6 thousand. That is a tremendous increase.
Dr. Wisenthal has also calculated the costs and his figures are startling. If you take university costs in 1961 and give them an arbitrary figure of $100, by 1969 this had increased to $507.7, an increase of more than 500 per cent. By 1980 this will increase to $3,181.5, more than 31 times as much as we were spending in 1961. I am one of those who over the years have called for better things in the way of education. According to the statistics given by Dr. Wisenthal it appears that we may be facing an actual expenditure of $8.3 billion on all forms of post-secondary education in 1980. I do not know if this country can find that amount of money, but it seems to me this projection raises a number of very important questions about which the federal government has not even begun to think.
If we find this money, must it be at the expense of sacrificing other programs which are equally or even more important? We know about the housing needs of people in the low-income bracket. We know about the housing needs of people in the middle-income bracket in cities such as Toronto and Vancouver. These people are not able to finance adequate housing for themselves. If we have to find the kind of money which Dr. Wisenthal talks about, we may not be able to fulfil the desire of the Canadian people for proper kinds of social security systems, for adequate pensions, for an extension of health services to include such things as dental care and mental health, and for a guaranteed income. With respect to the latter, it appears to be part of the programs of all political parties, although we may differ about the details and we certainly differ about the timing for the implementation of such a program.
All this has happened at a time when easy assumptions were made by people in the educational field and by political leaders of all parties, that an education pretty well guaranteed an interesting job at good pay. That was the case until recently, Mr. Speaker, but obviously it is not the case any more. I am sure there is not a member of Parliament who has not been faced in his own city by young people coming to him and saying they have a B.A., an M.A. or even, according to yesterday's Globe and Mail, a Ph.D. and yet they cannot find employment. A study conducted by Dr. Frank Kelly, science adviser to
[Mr. Orlikow.l
November 19, 1970

the Science Council of Canada, shows that fewer than half the people in Canada who will be granted Ph.D. degrees in engineering and science this year will find jobs next spring. I could give details of a study carried out by the Graduate Students Association of the University of Toronto. The study shows that not only will this happen this coming spring but in fact it happened last summer when half the Ph.D. graduates of the University of Toronto did not get a job and so went on to further post-doctoral studies.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
We are facing an extremely difficult situation, Mr. Speaker. I have raised some of the questions asked by Dr. Wisenthal. I take no credit for the Ontario government, which is not formed by the party to which I belong but is a Conservative government; however, it appointed a commission on post-secondary education in Ontario headed by Dr. Wright. This commission has made a preliminary report. Whilst they have not any more answers than I have, they have asked a number of very important questions which they intend to look into.
They asked why higher education must be carried out in institutions called universities and colleges. They asked why it would not be possible to have, in place of segregated and fragmented institutions, a plethora of educational services available to all, at any age. They asked why universities have to be conducted in such a way as to have summer holidays lasting several months. They asked why it is necessary for young people to go directly from high school to college, which means that a student has almost 20 years of continuous education. They asked whether in fact young people coming from poor or low-income families have been or are able to go to university in any substantial numbers; whether in fact we are subsidizing the children of middle and upper-income families, those best able to look after their own needs.
These are questions of importance in respect of all the educational programs of the federal government for the next couple of generations. I hope the federal government will stop simply paying what it has accepted as its share of the cost of higher education and will begin to involve itself seriously with the provinces in a co-operative study of the problems of higher education, where we are going and what we ought to do in the next couple of generations.

subsubtopic: MR. KNOWLES (WINNIPEG NORTH CENTRE)-OPENING OF PARLIAMENTARY RESTAURANT ON SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 21-REMUNERATION OF STAFF
speechtext:
Order, please. As the hon. member has indicated, he gave the Chair notice of the question of privilege. The Chair will, as the hon. member has suggested, discuss the details of the question of privilege with Mr. Speaker. I undertake to the hon. member and to all hon. members of the House that I will do that.

November 19, 1970
Employment Programs

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Stanfield:
That this House condemns the government for increasing the economic inequalities between different regions of Canada by its opposition to full employment policy and its refusal to use short-term and long-term programs in a timely and effective manner to prevent the resulting recession-level poverty and social injustice now widespread in Canada.
And the amendment thereto of Mr. Douglas (Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands).
Mr. Paul Yev/chuk (Athabasca): Mr. Speaker, generally speaking, unemployment and regional disparities can be discussed together because one is often dependent upon the other; they are two interdependent factors. In 1968 the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his party won the election. They won it partly on the promise, I think, that they would be instrumental in removing regional disparities within the country. Generally speaking, when somebody says he wants to do something about regional disparities, I take this to mean that he is going to make efforts to improve the condition of poverty-stricken areas, that is to say, to improve their economic status. At the same time I take this to mean the provision of more employment in those areas and that disparities will be wiped out because we should make economic conditions across this country uniform.
Unfortunately, the opposite has occurred. I think the government attempted to live up to its promise to remove regional disparities, but it is not doing it in the way I have described. What is happening is that areas of prosperity and high employment are being dragged down to the level of those areas where there is great poverty and high unemployment. This is paradoxical. The government has adopted the wrong approach in dealing with unemployment and regional disparities. It is important for us to recognize that if we are to reverse the trend that the government has begun, the government must follow a national economic policy based upon certain economic realities. It must do that if it is to achieve the desirable economic goals which the Economic Council of Canada has set, namely, full employment.
We consider that an unemployment rate of 3.8 per cent of the work force constitutes full employment, a high rate of growth, by which we mean an increase of approximately 4.75 per cent per year in the gross national product, and reasonable price stability, by which we mean that prices shall not increase by more than 2 per cent per year. Also, we must be in a viable balance of payments position in which the foreign exchange rate of our money is not subject to undue fluctuation. Finally, we must see to it that there is an equitable distribution of our rising incomes.

Unemployment affects different regions of the country differently. However, as obvious as this might appear, the government's policy has not been affected by this reality. Part of the difficulty, it appears, is that the government is obsessed with controlling inflation. Because of this position it has virtually ignored the very important side effects of its war on inflation. One of those consequences is the reduced capability of the economy. The economy has already fallen substantially below its potential. The second side effect is the high unemployment rate that we have in the country today.
Let us look at the unemployment figures for the various provinces. We see that the situation is extremely unhealthy at this time. In British Columbia, for example, projections are that unemployment this winter will be in the area of 13 per cent. In the Prairie region, which traditionally enjoys the lowest level of unemployment of any region of the country, projections point to an unemployment rate of 8 per cent, which is more than double the rate normally experienced in that region in the winter. In addition, there is reason to believe that there is a considerable amount of hidden unemployment in the Prairies because the labour force figures omit farmers who have been made idle because of the slowdown in farm production. The projection for Quebec is that more than 12 per cent of the work force will be unemployed this winter. For the Atlantic region, which traditionally suffers from the highest unemployment rate, the projections show an unemployment rate this winter as high as 14 per cent.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
The structural reasons for unemployment, such as remoteness from markets, aging population and reduced educational capabilities of the work force, have been seriously aggravated by the government's anti-inflation policy. It does no good for the government to saddle this region with the high costs of its anti-inflation campaign and then unsuccessfully try to offset these costs with an inadequate regional incentives policy. In order to properly tackle the questions of regional disparity and unemployment, a regional approach to this problem is needed. The fiscal and monetary policies of the government must be sensitive to the differences in the economic and social potential of Canada's regions. It is absurd to expect the Prairie and Atlantic provinces to pay the price of the government's fight against inflation when these regions are suffering the worst unemployment in years.
A regionalized approach toward inflation and unemployment would match the cure with the illness. The Atlantic, Prairie and British Columbia regions depend very heavily on international trade, particularly with respect to primary products. In June the government decided to float the value of the Canadian dollar. This action had very severe effects on regions involved in international sales of primary products. The government has contemplated no positive measures to alleviate the burden caused by this move. In addition, the existing tariff policy of Canada does little to help those regions which depend upon foreign trade in primary products.
November 19, 1970

Unemployment is high. This is one of the effects of the government's war on inflation. When we examine the situation we find it is a little paradoxical that the government is probably the greatest contributor to inflation. This can be illustrated by the fact that the government's spending and taxation policies will be the main inflationary causes for at least another couple of years. Direct taxes contribute greatly to rising costs and prices. However, that is only part of the story. Increased government spending was achieved by bidding away resources and people from private industry. The result has been to increase incomes and prices and to make these resources scarce in the private economy.
This inflationary pressure will probably continue, because even at this time government spending is greatly increasing. Business cannot continue much longer to absorb increased costs and defer price increases. Business profits are 14 per cent lower than they were a year ago. In manufactured goods, profits are down 27 per cent. Capital investment, and ultimately long-term productivity. appear to be in jeopardy. As I mentioned previously, the Prairie region is in difficulty.
A few days ago I was alarmed to see a report from the Department of Agriculture indicating that in 1969, Canada for the first time in history became a net importer of agricultural products. This development becomes even more startling when one compares the 1969 agricultural trade deficit of $35 million with a net agricultural export surplus balance of $826 million, which was achieved in 1966. Over the years we have traditionally had a favourable balance of trade in agricultural products, ranging from $200 million to the high of $826 million.
The reason for the current unfavourable balance is two-fold. First, a recognizable decline of exports has been recorded since the high registered in the mid-1960s, 95 per cent of which is attributed to wheat. Second, importation of agricultural products has risen by roughly 80 per cent since the mid-1950s while at the same time exports have increased by less than 30 per cent for the corresponding period. While the majority of the decrease in our exports was the result of our dismal sales performance in wheat, other grain sales were disastrously affected. As a matter of fact, exports of coarse grains, barley, oats and rye reached the lowest level in more than ten years, registering an export figure of $37 million compared with an average of $96 million recorded in the period 1955-59. I ask hon. members to recall which party was in power at that time.
Turning to the meat industry, we note another startling revelation. The year 1969 produced an unfavourable balance in the meat trade, recording imports of $121 million against exports of $76 million. Such a large discrepancy has never before occurred, although there were slight deficits recorded in the years 1963 and 1967. Imports of $121 million represents an increase of 538 per cent over the level established in the period 1955-59, while exports for the year represent an increase of 78 per

cent over the level established during the same period. Another fact which undoubtedly a vast majority of Canadians, especially farmers, find very difficult to accept-is that Canadians are now consuming some $60 worth of imported agricultural products annually, per capita, which is twice the amount for 1960.
When one analyses these figures, one wonders just what lies in store for the agriculture industry in the 1970s. The implications of the government's program to control production through restrictive quotas and national marketing measures, coupled with no-grow policies in respect of grains and the general concept of gearing production closer to domestic consumption, could very well inhibit the prospect of ever achieving a healthy, viable industry. We now have a grains policy which advocates the consolidation of farms into large, so-called commercially viable units. At this time, no one knows what farmers will do when they find they are forced to leave their farms. It will obviously add to the terrible unemployment situation which now exists. There appears to be no satisfactory program to cope with the retraining of these people and relocating them in satisfactory economic situations.
We have a marketing bill now before Parliament- which proposes to impose government controls on all aspects of production-buying, pricing, assembling, packing, processing, transporting, storing and determining the quantity, the time and place at which a regulated product may be produced. Why are such impositions being instituted? According to the experts and the government, the reason is that we have huge surpluses of agricultural products and we must institute quotas and other measures to ensure supply management and production control.
I believe this approach is sheer nonsense. What we need, first, is an admission by the government that the sales performance and marketing record of agriculture products has deteriorated to the point that it now must be classified as a dismal failure. I believe we then must take cognizance of the observation of the task force that our present allocation of funds to market research is far from adequate. In the past, a meagre 1.2 per cent of the total amount spent on all agricultural research programs has been allocated to market research, distribution and international trade. The task force also said that it found fotally incomprehensible the present lack of policies and priorities in the field of market research. It questioned whether the industry could withstand the vagaries to which it will be subjected without some clearly defined policies and goals. So evident was this that in several instances the task force was unable to secure adequate research data in Canada to compile its report and found that such information was more readily accessible from foreign sources, particularly the United States.
© (8:20p.m.)
I believe we should ask ourselves whether we in Canada wish to continue to be a net importer of agricultural products. If the answer is no, as I am sure it is, then it is the duty of the government and of the agricultural

November 19, 1970
Employment Programs
sector in general to establish some priorities. We have already proved we can produce. We have the land, we have the ability, we have the technology and we can produce efficiently.
The first priority, as I see it, is that government and the agricultural sector in general must allocate more resources to market research and place more emphasis on market information and the dissemination of this information. On the basis of such factual and comprehensive information, farmers throughout Canada will be able to achieve an effective degree of product diversification related to forecasts and surveys made of market potential at home and abroad. In addition, we need an aggressive and effective sales force, thoroughly knowledgeable with respect to our products and the needs of our customers, which would show distinct loyalty to the concept of Canada first.
In conclusion, I believe the government should reassess its spending and taxation policies and then take a fresh look at its approach to regional disparities which have been treated in a backwoods manner up to the present time.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 53-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED LACK OF POLICIES AND PROGRAMS TO PREVENT UNEMPLOYMENT, POVERTY AND SOCIAL INJUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, neither the no-confidence motion of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), nor the amendment of the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan The Islands (Mr. Douglas), are acceptable. Instead, we should congratulate the government for the steps taken to reduce regional disparties and what social injustices exist in Canada.
The Gaspe area, one of whose representatives I am in the House, has always been considered by Canadians generally as being economically weak, but offering great possibilities for industrial development. The situation that prevails in the Gaspe peninsula also exists in many other parts of Canada.
To all those questions, there is an answer; it is a matter of finding it. There is no reason why the people of the poorer areas should keep on living in a state similar to that of the 30s, even in eastern Quebec where neither farming nor the lumber industry are profitable in many cases.
Referring to the history of Gaspe, should we say or even think that the federal government is the only one to blame for the economic and social situation now prevailing?
In the 1930's, local authorities, very often the priests of various Gaspe parishes, made representations to governments for the formation of new parishes, most of the time under the pretext of developing natural resources such as agriculture and forestry. The undertaking met with doubtful success.
Indeed, lengthy studies revealed that the economy of such parishes or villages was not profitable and that the social atmosphere was very difficult for their inhabitants.
Once those parishes, called marginal, disappear, nothing will prevent the movement of the population towards well-established service centers where it will be possible to attract industries.
Such is the situation of people anxious to improve their lot and ready, through the policy of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, to take the necessary means to reach this aim.
It is difficult to admit that in 1970, a group of parish priests should endorse a manifesto more negative than positive urging the people to stay in marginal parishes where experience has proved that economic and social life is impossible. Why blame this government which does use every possible means in order to improve the living conditions of people likely to be displaced?
Mr. Speaker, the opposition criticizes the regional economic expansion policy of the government but, in my opinion, it is the only solution to achieve the suppression of economic disparit.es. In a few years, we shall admit that the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the hon. Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) were right.
Because of the experience gained in eastern Quebec as a result of the surveys carried out by the Eastern Quebec Development Agency (BAEQ) and following the Canada-Quebec agreement, we are looking forward to a general and gradual breakthrough during the next few months.
In spite of the delays, is it right for us to find fault exclusively with the central government which has been supporting its fair share of the financial burden? Should we not remember that during the past two years, while the Quebec government was responsible for the implementation of this agreement, some of the provincial ministers, ostensibly to preserve the territorial integrity of their province, tried along with some officials, to hinder the carrying out of individual projects provided for in the agreement, the financing of which was to be the responsibility of the federal government on a 75 per cent basis.
I do not have to recall those lengthy and hazardous discussions which set the provincial authorities against the federal government with respect to the development of the Forillon national park.
Are we to think then that, because the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) initiated the establishment of this park and had the funds required, the federal government is to be blamed if the agreement was signed two years late? I do not believe so. However, considering the attitude of Mr. Marcel Masse, provincial minister responsible for the Eastern Quebec Development Bureau at that time, the Quebec government is entirely to blame since it appeared, for numerous non valid reasons, to want to deprive the Gaspe population of an annual economic expansion worth from $30 to $40 million, when the national park is ready for use. Those figures do not appear to have been exaggerated, considering the experience of other provinces.

November 19, 1970

Every member nows that although it is underdeveloped, the Gaspe peninsula possesses considerable natural resources, which can be exploited with profit.
Would it be normal that in 1970 the Canadian government should venture to spend substantial amounts of money to create in every village of the Gaspe peninsula industries like the Gaspesia Pulp and Paper Company Ltd., in Chandler, and the Consolidated Bathurst Limited, in New Richmond? Is it not preferable to apply government policy, which consists in helping these lumber companies to expand and offer more jobs to the population, and consequently, enable it to reach a standard of living comparable to that of other regions with a stronger economy? This policy, which I consider acceptable, will make possible the establishment of service centres adequate to present needs. The policy we are trying to implement in the Gaspe peninsula should also be applied in the Atlantic provinces.
The government's regional development policy is aimed at ensuring for future generations a standard of living more in keeping with the economic progress of the nation as a whole.
The present government has already shown, and continues to show a keen interest in the establishment of new industries in Canada. Volvo, Michelin, Canadian General Electric are now operating in Nova Scotia and the leader of the Opposition, before presenting his motion of non-confidence, should have taken into consideration the benefits his own province has derived since 1963 from the federal government's policies.
The present government, through its Department of Regional Economic Expansion, has made it possible for existing companies to obtain grants for purposes of expansion. In this way the government participated financially in the expansion of several industries in my riding, including the Gaspesia Pulp and Paper Company Ltd. in Chandler, the Consolidated Bathurst Limited mill in New Richmond. It also helped the construction of the Canadian International Paper Company mills in Matane and, finally, it subsidized the fisheries complex in Riviere-au-Renard.
I would suggest that certain mining companies such as Noranda Mines and others decentralize some of their operations and install refining plants in underdeveloped areas. This decentralization would achieve two very definite objectives: the industrial development of such areas, which would ensure additional jobs and enable their residents to attain a living standard similar to that of the more favoured Canadian regions; and the possibility for decentralized plants to combat pollution of urban centers.
[DOT] (8:30p.m.)
For a long time, transportation has been a problem in several parts of Canada. For some years, the present government has endeavoured by all necessary means to meet all the requirements in this field. This goodwill on the part of the government is demonstrated by the fact that work has already begun on the site of the new Sainte-Scholastique airport.
Employment Programs
In the Gaspe and Lower St. Lawrence region alone, the federal government has spent, since 1964, $13 million for road construction, excluding the Trans-Canada Highway. It has built the ocean ports of Chandler, New Richmond, Matane and Riviere-au-Renard so as to allow the regular operation of the local industries, thus ensuring a decent standard of living for a good part of the population.
In conclusion, the motion moved by the hon. leader of the opposition and the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands are irrelevant in the present context.
In fact, after these remarks, it would appear that the government, in my view, is fully able to set priorities notwithstanding the stresses it has to face. The future will demonstrate that the right hon. Prime Minister and the members of his cabinet were working for the wellbeing of the nation as a whole.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 53-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED LACK OF POLICIES AND PROGRAMS TO PREVENT UNEMPLOYMENT, POVERTY AND SOCIAL INJUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the way the motion under consideration is now worded, gives hon. members the opportunity to point out, each in his own way, the poor results witnessed by the Canadian people concerning the unequal opportunities for a decent life in a country so affluent with a variety of all sorts of assets that its present administration is faced once more with an overproduction problem.
Instead of looking for a solution in the improvement of the means of distribution, a price and income commission was set up at the cost of $160,000 to $179,000 per year, in order to show to the Canadian people that they overspend. Here is an example of income distribution: a few good friends of the administration are paid salaries of $28,000, $33,000, $37,000 and $40,000 a year.
Several Canadians realize that it is a big price to pay to learn that they overspend. We learned lately that the members of the commission had succeeded in establishing, after investigation, the price of a cup of coffee. They would be of much greater service to the people if, while looking for price adjustment methods, they would try to uncover the true reasons for the price increases. They would easily find that one of those reasons is the high cost of interest on the public debt.
From confederation until 1964, the Canadian people have paid over $15 billion in interest on the public debt, and since then, the cost of interest on that famous debt has exceeded one billion dollars each year. Let us consider for one moment the tremendous increase of our debts and of all kinds of taxes which inevitably affect prices and we shall find the major cause for the increase in the cost of living.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
The higher the proportion of income absorbed by taxes the more the purchasing power of the consumer is decreased and, without noticing it, he is drifting towards state socialism.

November 19, 1970
Employment Programs
This is easy to understand: the money the taxpayer keeps he can spend at will while the tax money taken in by the government is spent by the state according to its own plans and not according to the individual's plans.
The federal government now takes more than 25 per cent of the citizens' income. It manages more than one quarter of the total expenditures in this country. It rules over a little more than one quarter of our production and our consumption.
To this must be added the share taken by the provincial and municipal governments. One can wonder whether this is leading to the forced abdication of the human being to governments. And yet, the human being is free, and the government is only an institution bound to his service.
Some complain of being overburdened by taxation and above all consider that they are being deprived of the fruit of their labour, and they have a good point. However, I wanted mostly to outline that steadily increasing taxes are leading us quickly to state socialism.
Besides, when the overburdened private enterprise loses heart, it is, of course, replaced by an industrial or a state monopoly. In the first case, we have financial domination, and in the second, state bureaucracy. A system must be quite out of gear to force a choice between those two forms of human enslavement.
However, there is another solution: the control of money where it originates, according to the facts, the rights of the human being, and the capacity of the country. This would be Social Credit. But our governments prefer to rule the individuals rather than interfere with the privileges of the people who create money.
It is true that unless we decide on reform according to the Social Credit theory, whether we like it or not, we are on the way to state socialism, including the degradation of the human being.
Socialism and communism approach the problem of the distribution of goods with the idea that some people have too little and others too much. Instead of requesting the distribution of all surplus products, which represent an unused collective share, they insist on taking away from those who seem to have more than their share.
Unfortunately, sociologists, labour leaders, even earnest supporters of corporatism, approach the distribution problem somewhat in the same light. Without falling into the excesses of a sour and levelling communism, they seek a solution to the social problem only in a less unequal distribution of goods, and not in a generous distribution of the goods not already apportioned.
They all follow the rule of work participation in order to have titles to production, while promoting a more equitable allocation of those titles. Their submission to that rule is the cause either of their errors, or their deficiencies, or their difficulties, because since man has been using his brains, he seeks to eliminate human labour from production. And in an age when he succeeds
more and more, the problem becomes harder and harder for those good researchers, however well-intentioned they might be. They all lack a clear understanding of the distributive economic doctrine of Social Credit.
Besides denouncing this paralyzing and debt-breeding tyranny of the monopoly of money and credit, we suggest means to end it.
As soon as one acknowledges that the realities to produce are there-and I believe that they are easy to see-one has to proceed to implementation. It will also have to be accepted that the implementation of the financial suggestions of Social Credit set forth by Major Douglas would eliminate the obstacles precisely by putting finance before those realities.
"Finance, as rightly stated by Major Douglas, must be controlled by production and consumption or the production and distribution of products should not be conditioned by finance."
Money and credit-the purchasing power-available to the people must be constantly equivalent to the total price of goods available in that country-whatever the cost price of such goods-and those means of payment must be cancelled or depreciated only in accordance with the consumption and depreciation of consumer goods.
Any new production must be financed with new credit which would be recalled and cancelled only according to the appreciation-depreciation ratio.
The distribution of the purchasing power among individuals must depend less and less on employment to take into account an increased production, while there is a reduction of manpower. Dividends must gradually replace wages as the production capacity increases through automation and improved machinery. We must set up a financial system whose application patterns may vary yet respect those principles, as opposed to the present system which is inappropriate and disorganized, which breeds hardships or worries, inertia or unpaid debts while there is boundless productivity. There no longer shall we complain about lack of schools, of houses or of other things to meet real public or private needs.
Progress thus put at the service of everybody, without any financial restrictions, will prevent man from becoming too preoccupied and too busy with economic matters. It will therefore be up to him alone to engage in free activities favouring full development of his personality. Evidently, there will remain a wide field of action for teachers and priests but, at least, limits to this full development will not be imposed any longer by financial decisions only. We will no longer suffer from a financial dictatorship rationing human beings despite plentifulness and paralyzing citizens despite efficient means of action.
If everyone knew really what it means to be an honest and hard working man who is a victim of unemployment and finds himself unable to provide his family with a decent living, through the fault of an obsolete economic system, many people would change their mind and those mummies left over from a past to be forgotten would

November 19, 1970

soon be revived through a live contact with the realities of today.
Some people are quick to state that the Creditistes have "forward" ideas. This could well mean an implicit condemnation of the position of those who prefer to mark time in a world continuously striving for new achievements. Should we, in order not to disturb those champions of an economic statu quo, burden the rest of humanity-the healthy part-with the unbearable weight of so-called dogmas, the work of human brains trying hard to be considered infallible?
Because of the present situation, it is obvious that this winter will bring a great deal of unemployment and that many regions will particularly be afflicted by it. Among the various classes of manpower, it is the younger and the older people who are the most hardly hit. These two classes of workers deserve special sympathy. If it is appropriate to seek the best means of solving the problem, a task which is everybody's concern, it might also be important to show some understanding for the unemployed, to avoid summary judgments and, mostly, to avoid taking advantage of the present situation to retaliate on the workers. The spectre of unemployment is hard enough to bear without that.
It happens that we take the young people to task for their lack of ambition and ideals and find them skeptical and blase. We also severely blame them for being heartless and lacking in initiative. Of course, too soft and too superficial an education or the search for easy living have degraded the taste for well being earned through sacrifice. But that could not be true in every case. Those who have grown up in a large family have already had the opportunity of learning the value of sacrifice and selfdenial. They soon learned how to take care of themselves. Those who had more than their share of hardships, those who had to make efforts to get a high school diploma or a university degree have already earned, through their will to succeed, a capital that others do not have.
Anxious to work and to build a successful future, they are faced at the start with an artificial system which raises obstacles in their path. They feel crushed and deprived of a fundamental right: the right to work. They feel useless. A large number of them keep hoping that tomorrow maybe they will be accepted on the job, like the immigrant to whom the door of the country is widely opened. He will remember this with sorrow and with resentment, unable to understand why he was turned down.
What is more serious still is that many, even thousands, face the same situation. To be sure, a distinction must be made between those who want to work and those who do not, between those who are lazy and those who are not, between those who are capable and those who cannot do any kind of work.
One fact remains: during the economic depression of the 30's young and not-quite-so-young people with ambition had a taste of what it meant to be jobless and to wait for prosperity over long years. Among them some had enough courage to face exile in order to find employ-
Employment Programs
ment, yet without brighter hopes than the expectation of three meals a day. Others had to wait for the war to break out in order to relieve their parents of the burden of a dependence very unwillingly imposed upon them.
Let us try and find solutions more in keeping with 1970 realities.
[DOT] (8:50p.m.)

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 53-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED LACK OF POLICIES AND PROGRAMS TO PREVENT UNEMPLOYMENT, POVERTY AND SOCIAL INJUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been looking forward to this opportunity to pass along to the government the expressions of great concern that my constituents are conveying to me in increasing numbers and with increasing urgency. It becomes more difficult with every day that passes to explain to my constituents why the government of our wealthy nation cannot provide the basic necessities of life for its citizens. It is not enough just to say to the unemployed that our country is being poorly managed. It is not enough to say to them that the present government is inept, inefficient and confused. If I were to offer no more than that, I would be doing the same as the government is doing; I would be offering words instead of action.
Since the government appears to be tragically unaware of the seriousness of the unemployment situation in this country and of the seriousness of the general economic climate in Canada today, I would like to lay on the table a few frightening examples of what we are faced with, in the hope that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) will take note of them. First of all, it will probably come as a surprise to the Minister of Finance to learn that his attack on inflation has been a disaster. It will probably come as a surprise to this government that the people of Canada are not smiling as broadly as the Minister of Finance when they contemplate the greatly increased unemployment that faces us in the coming winter months.
At the present time the rate of unemployment in Canada is the worst in 25 years. But according to the forecasts, that is only the beginning. The outlook for even our most affluent provinces, for the provinces with the best management, is dire indeed. Starting with the Atlantic provinces, the prospect is 14 per cent unemployment in the coming months, and some forecasts go up to 20 per cent. This is a high price to pay for the government's ill-conceived and ill-fated war against inflation.
In Quebec, the prospect is 13 per cent unemployment, and this figure is likely to be exceeded. There is a Liberal government in Quebec now, and even the attempts of the federal Liberal government to shore up

November 19, 1970
Employment Programs
Quebec's tangled economic situation is not likely to help matters a great deal. The federal government has accepted the responsibility to provide the jobs that the Premier of Quebec promised his people if he were elected, and it appears that both governments have failed miserably.
In the Prairie provinces the prospects are no better. It is predicted that unemployment in the three Prairie provinces will run to at least 8 per cent, and again this is a conservative estimate. Moving to the west coast, that western anchor of this great nation, this wealthy nation, the province of British Columbia faces the prospect of 12 per cent to 14 per cent unemployment at a time when jobs should be most plentiful.
Using the round figures of 500,000 unemployed and $5,000 as the annual income lost by each unemployed person, the net loss to the country is astronomical. This represents a loss of income in the order of $2J billion a year. Using a base tax rate of 10 per cent, the loss in taxes amounts to $250 million. The lost income represents lost purchasing power, lost opportunity for these people to better themselves in our society and lost dignity and pride of accomplishment.
We cannot afford a loss of this magnitude. If any corporation or business adopted the same shoddy business practices that this government is using to manage the country, that company or business would surely fail. The same logic must be applied to our country, because our country is a giant corporation that is being managed for its stockholders, the Canadian people. Any government that attempts to manage Canada as though it were five separate economic entities is inviting disaster, and that is just the manner in which this country is being managed.
Surely the government must be aware of the seriousness of the unemployment situation. The figures are there for them to see. If the average Canadian can assess the danger that faces us economically, surely our jovial Minister of Finance can see the danger. In an economic system such as ours we can consider that we are holding our own if we hold unemployment to about 3.8 per cent, but only if we maintain an economic growth rate of about 4.5 per cent per year. We are tragically short of a healthy growth rate, at approximately 1 per cent, and we are certainly exceeding the limits of unemployment. In fact, that rate is more than double the acceptable rate.
There is clear evidence that the government does in fact recognize the danger in our economic and fiscal postures, in spite of its attempts to cover up with a smile and a shrug of the shoulder. There is evidence of panic in the ivory tower. There is clear evidence that the largest cabinet in the history of this country is slogging hopelessly in a morass of indecision and confusion. This confused situation is being compounded daily by the implementation of hastily contrived, stop-gap measures in a vain attempt to stem the tide.
One example of such hastily conceived measures is the streamlining of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. In the process, hundreds of local commission offices were closed and thousands of qualified persons have been required to deal at a distance with offices that are there for the sole purpose of serving the people. Every day I
receive requests from constituents for assistance in cutting through a new brand of red tape in order to obtain benefits that are rightfully theirs, benefits that have been paid for over many years. The percentage of cases in which I have been able to gain satisfaction for my constituents has been almost 100 per cent. This in itself points up the extent to which this particular management innovation has failed. However, it is useless to try to convince the government that other methods should be instituted.
The government is much too busy innovating and experimenting to concern itself with serving the Canadian individual. It is much easier to jump from one stop-gap measure to another than to try to develop long-range programs that work to the advantage of the individual. I am sure that the Liberal backbenchers receive the same type of complaints from constituents as do opposition members. It surprises me that there is so little evidence of concern on the part of those members with regard to government practices and government failures to resolve fundamental problems. It surprises me that at least a few government members do not take advantage of their rights under our parliamentary system to make their views known to their government.
It is typical that when the government announces loudly a program to deal with a problem, it tells only half the story. I am thinking about the program announced a few days ago to deal with unemployment. Included in the program is the provision of $10 million add tional funds for the Unemployment Insurance Commission retraining program. One would automatically assume that this would mean additional schoolroom seats for those who would like to improve their level of schooling and their employability. Speaking for Ontario, that is not the case. In response to complaints from constituents who were unable to enrol in a retraining course, I made inquiries about the state of the program in my area. I found that the budget for my region is short of its basic requirement by approximately $89,000 and, as a result, several levels of formal schooling have been wiped out for the present and for the foreseeable future.
* (9:00 p.m.)
For instance, two of the most important levels as far as improvement of employability are concerned, grades 11 and 12, have been eliminated from the training centres in my region. There are four classroom seats available in grade 8, and only one seat in grade 7. The number of job-seekers in the region has doubled in the past few months. The need for retraining has increased correspondingly, yet there has been a serious setback in retraining funds and facilities.
There is another aspect of the compound problem of economic slowdown and high unemployment that should be stressed, and that is the long-range effect of decreased revenue on the one hand and a spiralling welfare budget on the other. When people are unemployed for long periods of time, people who would ordinarily be employable, the drain on the public treasury for welfare and other assistance will in time create a serious imbalance in our economic structure. When people who should be

November 19, 1970

contributing to the economy are, instead, drawing from that economy, those who are contributing will be required to contribute still more. If this process served to eliminate the problem, it might be acceptable. But all it does is perpetuate the problem and we have a gradual roll-back in the economy instead of healthy growth.
As I mentioned before, Mr. Speaker, this situation cannot be prolonged indefinitely, not in a business or in a corporation and certainly not in a national economy. The fact remains that poor management is behind most of this country's ills. It is also a fact that the only way we can recover from the dilemma of impoverished affluence is to institute sound management principles. It would behove us to move in that direction now, while we can still move at all.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 53-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED LACK OF POLICIES AND PROGRAMS TO PREVENT UNEMPLOYMENT, POVERTY AND SOCIAL INJUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in order to develop those parts of our country which have experienced relative disfavour in the past, the government adopted certain programs under the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. I was overjoyed to see those programs adopted and I embraced them. The theory that money should be pumped into those areas to a greater degree than into the more developed centres is a sound one, but I wonder how it works in practice; I wonder if the end result is what we intended by bringing in that kind of measure.
Earlier in the debate many hon. members spoke about the incentives plan. The hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees), and I have great regard for his selling ability, particularly when he was the Minister of Trade and Commerce-he and his executive assistant had many great ideas for selling Canadian products-spoke about the industrial incentives plan and about other plans to be added to it. Regardless of what we add to that plan, I am wondering if the end that we seek is being accomplished. We hear murmurings from different parts of the country about whether the incentives plan really does develop the kind of industry, and therefore the kind of employment, we would like to see in those parts of the country that are less favoured than others.
How does it actually work, Mr. Speaker? The government comes along with a plan and says, "These areas are less favoured. If industries would like to establish in them, we will give certain amounts of money as an incentive for them to do so." But what in fact happens? I speak, as we say in French, en connaissance de cause, because northern Ontario has been established as one of those areas largely because of the efforts that some of us made to bring attention to that part of Canada. But there are many people who ask, "Even though northern Ontario is a designated area, just how much money has come into it for regional economic expansion?" If we make comparisons, and some people have done this, we see that some parts of Quebec have received more money. But let us look at this matter a little more closely. Let us look at my own constituency of Cochrane. Let us look at the various areas which could support new industries.
Employment Programs
I believe that no economic base is sound unless it maintains a variety of industries. A one-industry town is not economically sound, and this is the basis of many towns in northern Ontario. When you visit these towns and ask, "How would you like to have a new industry?" they reply, "By all means. We will do everything possible to help bring in a new industry." But, Mr. Speaker, when it comes down to the nitty-gritty, how many of those people have actually gone out and done something about bringing in industry?
I am raising these points because I do not know anyone who has put more effort into attracting secondary industry to northern Ontario than I have, and I have travelled all over the world. You just do not sit back and say, "We are a nice area. We have lots of nice fishing and hunting. Everybody should be happy to come here and establish industry." It does not quite work that way. Even with the incentive provided by the federal government of up to 25 per cent of the capital cost, how many people say, "We would like to go to northern Ontario"? There are not many who say that.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
It is a question of selling them the idea, bringing them there and letting them see what we have to offer in the region. Then perhaps they may establish a new industry. We have asked people from outside the country to put money into industries in that area, but the point is that unless there is some kind of input from local individuals, from local governments, and co-operation among all levels of government, we will not develop secondary industry in northern Ontario or anywhere else in Canada. It would be an anathema for us to speak against the idea of foreign capital in northern Ontario because we know we have no alternative source of capital. The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), has spoken on this subject. I suggest that those members of the New Democratic Party who are so ready to speak against foreign investment in this country should stop and think for a moment. No one in northern Ontario would stand behind that idea. It is strange that people in the New Democratic Party are so anxious to speak against American investment in Canada, or any kind of foreign investment but they specify American investment, of course.

expansion handout. I consider it a straight handout and it is a great thing. speechtext:
The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) has lit upon the question I was going to raise next, that is, transportation. In my wanderings around the world I came across a group willing to go into a pulp and paper enterprise in northern Ontario, which is something the local people cannot go into because it requires a large amount of capital, and so on. This is a case where you have to accept somebody else coming in. We hope this industry will come about. There are economic studies being made now to determine whether we should go into it.
One thing that concerns them and everyone who thinks about establishing in the northern part of Ontario and other regions of Canada which are disfavoured is the question of transportation, the question of freight rates. This is an essential program. Every time we speak about development we come back to the problem of freight rales, the cost of sending the products to market.

speechtext:
For this reason we hope very shortly to have a conference in northern Ontario which will determine a new transportation policy for the whole of that area. For the moment, however, let us consider one of the existing industries there, pulp and paper. Why should companies in Cochrane, Smooth Rock Falls, Kapuskasing, Timmins or anywhere in northern Ontario be jeopardized because of their location? Why should they have to spend more than someone in another part of the country to send their products to market? A producer in British Columbia can send his products to Europe much more cheaply than a producer from northern
Ontario, yet the British Columbia producer has to ship through the Panama Canal and across the ocean. In Germany, from anywhere along the Rhine River to the North Sea the cost of sending the product is the same. Of course, Germany is much smaller than Canada, but the principle is there. The point is that no one is jeopardized because he lives in one part of the country rather than another. Why should we in Canada be jeopardized in this way?
It seems to me that these disparities will not be cured by this program of incentives alone. We have to look deeper. The real problem is transportation. This is a big country and we cannot send products to the sea from every part of it for the same price. But we should be able to do so and there should be a policy established for that purpose, otherwise people in one part of the country are disfavoured as compared with people in another part.
In years past, Mr. Speaker, we have heard these problems discussed. People have said, "We in northern Ontario are not understood by people in the south. People in Toronto don't know about us, don't care about us; they forget about us."

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have before us a motion which, among other things, refers to the increasing economic inequalities among different regions of Canada. For the purpose of my remarks tonight I should like to state that there are four regions of Canada. The first is the metropolitan megalopolis like that to which the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Stewart) referred. Those of us who live in other places feel they are such vast centres of power and luxury that the rest of us are hewers of wood and drawers of water for the city dweller. However, I have heard the hon. member for York West (Mr. Givens) say that the second heaven has not yet arrived for people in places like Toronto. I have to agree. I would not want to live in one of those asphalt jungles.
We are considering the responsibilities of the federal government and what it has accepted as its responsibilities in dealing with the inequalities of various regions of Canada. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that there are specific

November 19, 1970

policies to make provision for such things as urban renewal, urban reconstruction and that sort of thing in the urban regions of Canada. Then we have what have been referred to as the slow-growth areas of the country. These are areas where for one reason or another it would appear the economy has become stagnant and unemployment has reached unusually high levels. In respect of these regions we have had much debate for many years in the House. Various types of programs have been tried and developed, and some have been discarded. At present we have ARDA and we had the designated areas program. Now we have the designated regions under the regional Area Development Incentives Act.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
The third region I refer to constitutes 30 or 40 per cent of the land mass of Canada. It is the area of the territories. There, for constitutional reasons that I will not go into, the federal government has assumed great responsibilities, both in the area of industrial resource development and toward the provision of community facilities, to make it possible for the people who live and work in those areas to enjoy a reasonable standard of living. There again we may say that perhaps everything is not all that it might be.
I suggest the fourth region of this country is what I will refer to as the fast-growth resource area, which is largely in the northern parts of the provinces. The hon. member for Cochrane referred to one of these areas. These areas, for one reason or another, feel alienated from our great metropolitan regions such as Toronto or Vancouver. The area that I represent, which is roughly the northern three-quarters of Vancouver Island, is one such area. It is not a matter of redevelopment; it is not a matter of the existence of a high level of unemployment in those areas: it is a matter of beginning with undeveloped resources and undeveloped facilities and of people having to live there and of travel to and from the area.
I have been examining various programs of the federal government. It seems to me that the whole area of the country which has sometimes been referred to as a possible mid-Canada corridor has really been left out of the picture so far as concerns economic inequalities and social inequalities that may exist between this region and the other regions of Canada I have outlined. Therefore, I think it is time that a few minutes were taken to examine this situation.
The only existing federal programs in those areas that I can think of are programs under the auspices of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in the fields of housing, and sewer construction which have general application across the country. I suppose one could say that the manpower retraining and mobility programs do something toward providing skilled manpower in those areas, but I suggest that these programs tend to aggravate rather than improve matters involving the provision of social amenities, transportation and other necessary facilities. This is a situation which I have discussed in the House and have raised with members of various federal governments over many years.
Employment Programs
I must say that it has been a rather frustrating task so far as I am concerned because I come from the province of British Columbia. It seems to me that this is something in which the government of the province of British Columbia has been completely uninterested. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, when we talked about the need for federal assistance in the provision of community facilities and transportation facilities in areas such as the northern part of Vancouver Island it was pretty difficult to build a convincing case when the Premier of British Columbia was talking not so long ago about having $300 million to pour into the Yukon if that part of Canada would link itself with British Columbia. That was $300 million for the building of highways and other community facilities.
