That is an example of the kind of problem that a member in the federal House representing such a fast growing area has had to face. There has been a need to examine the situation and to determine whether specific and particular problems and inequalities applied to the people living in those areas of the country, and to determine whether they need a distinctive program apart from that provided for slow-growth areas or for the great metropolitan centres.
There has been a glimmering of interest in this matter since the special areas were established under the government reorganization bill of the previous session. I am referring to the bill which established the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. The minister of municipal affairs has suggested that northern Vancouver Island is one of the areas that should qualify under this program. My initial reaction to that, Mr. Speaker, was that the suggestion probably did not amount to much more than the kind of sparring that had gone on between the federal and provincial authorities. I mention, for example, the idea which was bandied about of making the road to northern Vancouver Island part of the trans-Canada highway. I have suggested more than once that this proposition was never properly put to Ottawa and that if Mr. Bennett had $300 million to spend in the Yukon, he could certainly afford to build 100 miles or so of road northerly on Vancouver Island.

speechtext:
However, Mr. Speaker, this does not alter the fact that there is a real need for social capital to be invested in roads, sewer and water systems and in the normal paving programs that take place in communities. Also, when large industrial undertakings move in to exploit resources almost overnight, without any particular provision being made by any authority for a comparable investment to be made in community facilities, the people who are expected to live and work in these areas will be faced with real problems and, I submit, with real inequalities. So I suggest that when we talk about these programs to deal with such problems in specific regions of the country, consideration must and should be given to

November 19, 1970
Employment Programs
the particular needs of the people who live in the undeveloped, fast-growth resource areas in the northern parts of the provinces of this country.
I should like to see more serious attention paid to these problems. If the statements I have read in the press are correct, that the government of the province of British Columbia through a cabinet committee is making at long last a serious study of this problem with a view to making a presentation to the federal government in a proper way, I hope that that presentation will be given consideration by the government. I could expand on this situation in some detail. I could particularize those areas in my constituency where the need for this kind of development is the greatest. In the circumstances, and with the limited time I have in this debate, I do not think I have an adequate opportunity to develop this theme. I have, therefore, contented myself with giving a general outline of the problem which I submit exists virtually across the whole of Canada. It is one which, as I have already said, is of particular urgency in the area of Canada that I represent in this House.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it was only a few short years ago, 1961-1962, that the government of that day was being violently attacked in this chamber by those who now form the government because of the serious unemployment problem that confronted the country. Day after day, with their usual bloodthirsty motivation for political advantage, the Liberal opposition of those days-

speechtext:
bringing pressure on the economy have been compelled by their membership to press for higher and higher wages to replace lost purchasing power. This is the situation created by this government's policy of high taxes, high costs and high prices. It is a ruinous, iniquitous policy and has resulted in forcing down the standard of living of a whole group of Canadians who have joined the rank of the new poor as a result of this government's policies.
Inflation picks the pocket of the working man, siphoning purchasing power from his pay cheque, forcing him to demand higher and higher wages, taking the food away from his family. And that inflation is the product of policies of high taxation and high spending invoked by this government, which have subtracted the working man's gains at both ends by reducing the amount he receives and adding to the cost of the things he buys. Under this government labour has become the forgotten department. Labour has been downgraded. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) has been reduced to chief conciliation officer for the federal government. He is the closest thing to a minister without portfolio. These are the areas and these are the problems where the government has failed pitiably.
We have growing unemployment, the iniquitous indirect tax of forced inflation, high costs, unjustified government spending resulting in high taxation, with Canadians being squeezed more and more every day and having to run faster just to stay where they are. This is the area in which the government should act and in which it stands indicted by a record of inaction unparalleled in the history of this nation. This government should come back to earth, forget about long-range theorizing and academic abstractions and come to grips with the people's problems. They should stop preening and admiring themselves. They are all on a permanent ego trip. Where is the just society? What happened to the war on poverty? Where is participatory democracy? Slick phrases coined to get votes, but principles forgotten. Poverty cannot be beaten without full employment. Society cannot be just, with poverty increasing.
This government has been spending hundreds of thousands, nay, millions of dollars on armies of task forces running all over the country, to say nothing of the commissions and royal commissions. The Prime Minister, his ministers and most members on the government side have been busy mounting platitudes and paying lip service to the just society, participatory democracy and the now infamous war on poverty in the various regions of Canada. Since all these task forces, commissions and royal commissions, studies and reports have a name, I think we should give a name to the government's efforts to fight the war on poverty, a name to describe the things being said by government spokesmen in their posture of being great generals riding to do battles which they have not even begun. Let us call their efforts and their statements "combined regional anti-poverty." The true measure of their efforts and the truth of their statements may be best described, I suggest, by the first letters of each of four words of that title.
